docs.title: Circle Care Product Wiki
docs.text:
Care, in one circle. Circle Care is a privacy-first care-coordination app for an older adult who lives at home, the professional and family caregivers who help them, and the legal guardian who makes decisions with them. It puts everyone on the same daily plan — medicines, tasks, visits, check-ins and emergencies — while the older adult stays in charge of who can see what. This wiki documents the product end to end: why it exists, who it serves, every feature in the working prototype, how it is built and secured, and what comes next.

Concept product — fictional people and data

Circle Care is a portfolio and training product created by Sumanth (Product Owner, Certified Scrum Product Owner) from a CSPO course assignment. Every person, phone number, address, medicine and health reading in the prototype and in this wiki is fictional. No real health information is collected, stored or sent anywhere.

docs.title: Circle Care in 30 seconds
docs.text: What One app with three experiences — elder, caregiver and legal guardian — plus a marketing website. Installable on a phone as a Progressive Web App (PWA). Who Margaret "Maggie" Lee (80, lives alone in San Francisco), her daughter and healthcare power of attorney Sarah, her home care aide Ana, her grandson James, and a time-limited respite caregiver, Ruth. Problem Care for an older adult at home is split across texts, paper notes, phone calls and memory. Doses get missed or doubled, nobody knows who is covering tonight, and the older adult loses privacy and control. Answer A shared daily plan, gentle reminders, verified caregiver check-ins, a self-drafting shift hand-off, a hold-to-send SOS that escalates until someone answers, and a Privacy Center where the elder sees and controls access. Principles Privacy-first · Elder in control · Minimum necessary access. Status Working prototype v0.4. Care data runs entirely in the browser with encrypted demo data; an accounts server handles sign-in, profiles and test payment methods. No real notifications, not for real patients. North Star Verified care tasks completed on time per week — shown on the guardian's home screen and weekly digest. The public website introduces the product and links into the demo app.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Most older adults want to keep living in their own home. Doing that safely usually depends on a small, informal team: an adult child who handles medical and legal decisions, a paid home care aide for a few hours a day, and other relatives who help on weekends. That team rarely shares one source of truth.

  • Medicines are the highest-risk part of the day. A missed blood-pressure tablet or a double dose of a diabetes medicine is easy when three people are involved and nobody can see what the others did.
  • Coverage is fragile. A late or absent caregiver is often discovered hours later. Uncovered evening shifts go unnoticed until they arrive.
  • Emergencies depend on one phone call being answered. If the first person doesn't pick up, there is no automatic next step.
  • Privacy and dignity are an afterthought. Existing tools tend to treat the older adult as a patient being monitored, not as the person whose information it is.
  • Decision-makers are remote. A legal guardian who lives two hours away learns about problems days later, from someone else.

Circle Care's research plan (see Research & Compliance) frames these as hypotheses to validate with interviews; the prototype exists to make those conversations concrete.

docs.title: Who it serves and what each person gets
docs.text:
Elder (Maggie)Caregiver (Ana)Legal guardian (Sarah)

Value: independence with a safety net.

  • A home screen with exactly three large actions: What's next, SOS, Call my person.
  • Spoken reminders, three text sizes, high contrast and 48 px+ touch targets.
  • A one-tap daily "I'm OK" check-in instead of a worried phone call.
  • A Privacy Center to see who has access, who looked at her information, pause sharing and remove people.
  • Sees every decision made about her care and can ask a question.

Value: know exactly what this shift needs.

  • Check in at the door; today's medicines and tasks unlock only for the shift.
  • Doses in time order with Due now / Late / Overdue states and high-priority medicines called out.
  • Reads the previous caregiver's hand-off before starting.
  • At check-out the hand-off note is drafted automatically from what was logged.
  • Two-week schedule, shift offers and swap requests.

Value: peace of mind from a distance, without micromanaging.

  • Today at a glance: check-in, doses, tasks, who is with Maggie now, health and next appointment.
  • A short Needs your attention list instead of a stream of notifications.
  • Approvals for medicine changes, new members and shift swaps — Maggie sees every decision.
  • Health readings (only while Maggie shares them), a medication-appointment calendar and a weekly digest.
  • Care circle management, SOS order, alert timing and quiet hours.

docs.title: Product principles
docs.text:
1. Privacy-first

Health information stays inside the app. Lock-screen notifications and emails never name a medicine, condition or note. Data is encrypted on the device, every access is logged in a tamper-evident chain, and exports are passphrase-protected.

2. The elder is in control

The circle is built around one person. Maggie confirms members, sees who looked at her information, can pause sharing with one switch (SOS still works), decides whether her health readings are shared, and is told about every decision made about her. Refusing a medicine is recorded as her choice, not as an error.

3. Minimum necessary

Each role sees only what it needs. Professional caregivers see medicines and tasks only while checked in to a shift. Notes can be shared with everyone or with the guardian only. Guardian powers depend on verified legal documents. One permission matrix (src/data/policy.ts) decides every read and write.

docs.title: Document control
docs.text: Field Value Owner Sumanth — Product Owner (CSPO) Version 1.0 Date 2026-10-19 Status Approved draft Applies to Circle Care prototype v0.4 (commit 428fa2e) Review cycle Update with every release; the code is the source of truth when they disagree

docs.title: Regulatory Applicability Memo
docs.text: Notion stories: CC-8 counsel's review of this memo (not started), CC-196 this update Status: DRAFT v2 for counsel review, updated 2026-11-15 — not legal advice. v1 was written by the product owner from general knowledge on 2026-10-19, before Sprints 11 to 13 added real accounts, Social Security numbers, bank accounts, cards, profile photos, the family chat with voice replies, daily check-ins, supply counts and the evening recap. v2 adds those (§2.1, §10) and questions Q14 to Q25, and was checked against the data inventory (CC-9). No lawyer has reviewed it. Every conclusion below is a working assumption to be confirmed or corrected by qualified counsel before launch or pilot.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text: Identify which laws likely apply to Circle Care, under which business models, so the backlog includes the right controls and counsel's time is focused on the right questions.

docs.title: 2. Product facts relevant to the analysis
docs.text:
• Circle Care stores, for one older adult ("the elder"): medication list and schedule, dose logs (taken/skipped/refused), care tasks, visit check-ins, care notes, uploaded documents (care plans, discharge summaries, legal authority documents), an emergency card (allergies, conditions, directives, blood type), SOS events, daily check-ins, and an access log. See CC-9 data inventory.
  • Users: the elder, a verified legal guardian/healthcare POA, family members, professional caregivers (agency-employed or private), and an internal review team that verifies legal documents.
  • Channels: in-app, push, SMS, email. Lock-screen and email text is designed to carry no health information (CC-31; Digest email "carries no PHI").
  • Since Sprint 11 the prototype has a server and a Postgres database for real accounts: each person's name, contact details, email and password, profile photo and Social Security number, and the legal guardian's bank account and cards (see Accounts, identity & payments). Payments run through a simulated vault, no money moves, and outside production only test numbers are accepted (CC-182). The care circle itself (medicines, chat, check-ins) is still demo data kept in the browser, with fictional people. This memo is about the production product.

docs.title: 2.1 Data added since the October draft
docs.text:
Two business models, as in §3: Consumer, where a family uses Circle Care on its own, and Agency, where a home-care agency that is a HIPAA covered entity provides it to its clients. Each row matches a row of the data inventory's tables for these data types, except voice replies and the account email and password, which come from the code and the Postgres accounts table. Every cell is a working assumption for counsel to confirm.

Data Consumer model Agency model Working assumption Questions Social Security number Applies. Elder, caregiver and guardian accounts all hold one Applies the same way, including agency caregivers' accounts Not health data, but state SSN protection and data-security laws and every state's breach law cover it on its own, whatever the model. Collecting it at all needs a stated purpose Q14, Q15, Q22, Q24 Bank account Applies. Only the legal guardian adds one, to pay for care by ACH; a guardian's profile isn't complete without one, and the only one can't be removed Applies if the agency bills families through Circle Care Payment rules (Nacha, Regulation E) and money transmission law depend on who moves the money; GLBA may apply if Circle Care counts as a financial institution. A guardian paying for care from the elder's money may have to account for it Q16, Q17, Q22, Q24, Q25 Card Applies. Only the legal guardian adds cards, up to 5 Applies if the agency bills through Circle Care PCI DSS applies by contract with the card brands. The plan is to tokenize with Stripe so full numbers stay out of Circle Care's systems, but the Stripe path isn't built yet: today the development vault receives full test numbers in Circle Care's own server process Q16, Q17, Q23 Profile photo Applies to every account Applies; a full-face photo of a client is likely PHI under a BAA No face matching is done, so biometric laws likely don't apply today. A photo sent straight to the API keeps its location data (data inventory action) Q18 Family chat messages Applies. Free text that can hold health details Applies once an agency caregiver is added to the chat Treated as health data: consumer health data under state laws and the HBNR in consumer mode, PHI under a BAA in agency mode, though which messages a BAA covers is unclear (Q3) Q3, Q12, Q19 Voice replies in chat Applies when any member speaks a reply; the elder's chat has a large microphone button Applies, including agency caregivers' replies The chat's speech recognition doesn't ask the browser to stay on the device, so it may send the speaker's voice to the browser maker's servers. Only the text is stored, but sending the audio may be a disclosure to a third party, and the chat says the words are turned into text on the device (CC-222) Q20 Daily check-ins Applies. How the elder feels, water and meals Applies if caregivers or the agency see them Consumer health data; the elder chooses whether the guardian sees them, and a day logged while not sharing stays private Q21 "I'm OK" check-ins Applies (in the October draft); now with an optional mood Applies; likely PHI where agency caregivers see them The mood makes it health data, like the daily check-ins Q9, Q21 Supply counts Applies. Pills left and refill requests reveal which medicines the elder takes Applies; caregivers on shift can see and update them Health data. The app records that someone asked the pharmacy; it doesn't contact the pharmacy itself — Evening recap Applies; only the legal guardian sees it Applies the same way Nothing new is stored; it is worked out each time from data above. Its alert text carries no health details Q21 Account email and password Applies to every account Applies to agency staff accounts too Several states' breach laws treat an email plus its password as breach-triggering data on its own. Passwords are stored only as hashes Q22

docs.title: 3.1 When HIPAA likely does not apply directly
docs.text: HIPAA applies to covered entities (health plans, clearinghouses, providers who conduct standard electronic transactions) and their business associates. When a family downloads Circle Care and uses it on its own, Circle Care is likely a consumer health app, not a covered entity or business associate, even though it holds health information.

docs.title: 3.2 When Circle Care likely is a business associate
docs.text: Scenario Likely status (to confirm) A home-care agency that is a HIPAA covered entity contracts with Circle Care to coordinate its clients' care Circle Care = business associate of the agency; BAA required A health system or Medicaid waiver program offers Circle Care to patients and receives data back Likely business associate A private-pay caregiver (not a covered entity) uses Circle Care HIPAA likely does not apply via that caregiver An agency that does not bill electronically (may not be a covered entity) Unclear — counsel question Q2 Mixed: one circle includes an agency caregiver (BA relationship) and family (consumer) Unclear which data is PHI under the BAA — Q3

docs.title: 3.3 Plan: operate as HIPAA-ready regardless
docs.text:
Because the business model may include agencies, and because the same data is equally sensitive either way, Circle Care plans to meet the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules as a design standard for all circles:

  • Security Rule safeguards: risk analysis (CC-79), access control (CC-18/19), audit controls (CC-28), integrity, transmission security, workforce training, contingency planning.
  • Minimum necessary: caregivers see the plan only on shift (pro@shift).
  • Individual rights mirrored as product features: access/export (CC-32), access log (CC-29), amendment (open: no "request a correction" flow yet).
  • BAAs with every vendor that may touch health data (CC-30).
  • Breach response (CC-34).

The public Privacy page already states this posture ("designed to the HIPAA standard… even where HIPAA doesn't legally apply"). Counsel must review that wording before it is used publicly (Q1).

docs.title: 4. FTC Act §5 and the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (HBNR)
docs.text:
• Section 5 (unfair or deceptive practices): every privacy promise on the website and in the app is a representation the FTC can enforce. The "Things we will never do" list on /privacy must be true in production (e.g., "Use analytics that can identify a person"). Track each promise as a testable requirement.
  • HBNR (16 CFR Part 318): applies to vendors of personal health records and related entities not covered by HIPAA. As amended (2024), it is understood to cover health apps that draw information from multiple sources; Circle Care draws from the elder, caregivers and family (now also through the chat, voice replies and daily check-ins), and possibly device/health integrations later. A "breach" includes unauthorized disclosures, not only hacks — e.g., sharing with an analytics vendor without authorization.
  • Implication: in consumer mode, a breach could require notice to individuals, the FTC and possibly media. Timelines differ from HIPAA. Counsel to confirm (Q4). Sending voice audio to a speech service without authorization could itself count as a breach under this definition (Q20).
  • New promises to track: "ACH bank transfers have no platform fee", and that SSNs and full bank and card numbers are never shown or stored in full.
  • A promise that isn't true today: the chat's voice sheet says "Your words are turned into text on this device", but the chat doesn't ask the browser to recognize speech on the device, unlike the medicine voice check. Until story CC-222 fixes the code or the wording, this is a deception risk under Section 5 (Q20).

docs.title: 5. State laws (examples, not exhaustive)
docs.text: Law Why it may apply Product implications (to confirm) Washington My Health My Data Act (MHMDA) Covers "consumer health data" of WA residents, broadly defined; private right of action Separate consumer health data privacy policy; consent before collection and separate consent before sharing; right to delete; no geofencing near health facilities; restrictions on selling. Visit check-in uses location — confirm how (Q6). Similar state health-data laws (e.g., Nevada, Connecticut amendments) Similar consumer health data concepts Maintain a state-law tracker California CMIA May apply to businesses offering software designed to maintain medical information for consumers Confidentiality obligations; restrictions on disclosure California CCPA/CPRA Applies if thresholds are met; "sensitive personal information" includes health Notice at collection, right to limit use of sensitive PI, deletion, access State breach notification laws All states; many include medical information Track state-by-state timelines in CC-34 State guardianship/POA statutes Validity and scope of authority vary by state See §8 State EVV rules (Medicaid personal care) If agencies use Circle Care for Medicaid visits Circle Care is not an EVV system; don't market as one State SSN protection laws (e.g., California, Connecticut, Michigan, New York) Circle Care collects SSNs from elders, caregivers and guardians Limits on displaying, mailing and transmitting SSNs; some states require a published SSN privacy policy. Today the full number is never shown and is stored only encrypted (CC-180, CC-181). Confirm which states need a policy (Q14) State biometric privacy laws (e.g., Illinois BIPA, Texas, Washington) Only if profile photos or voice are ever used to recognize a person No face or voice matching today; consent would be needed before any is added (Q18, Q20) State data-security laws (e.g., Massachusetts 201 CMR 17.00, New York SHIELD Act) Circle Care holds residents' SSNs and bank account details A written information security program, vendor oversight and encryption duties, whatever the health-law answer (Q24) State money transmission laws Only if Circle Care itself holds or moves money between the guardian and caregivers or agencies Use a licensed processor that holds the funds; confirm the structure before money moves (Q16)

docs.title: 6. TCPA (SMS and calls)
docs.text:
• SMS reminders and alerts to circle members are likely informational, but TCPA consent rules still apply for automated texts to mobile numbers.
  • Plan: obtain express consent per phone number at invite acceptance (CC-17), honor STOP/HELP, record consent with timestamp, respect quiet hours (default 22:00–07:00 in settings.quietHours; SOS bypass is a design choice to review — criticalBypass).
  • Elder's number may be entered by a guardian: confirm who can consent on the elder's behalf (Q8).
  • SMS carries no PHI by design. SOS SMS fallback (via: "sms-fallback") must also be PHI-free.
  • Carrier registration (10DLC) and provider terms — operational, not legal, but blocks launch.

docs.title: 7. Accessibility — ADA and WCAG
docs.text:
• The prototype aims for WCAG 2.2 AA (README). Title III's application to apps and websites is subject to evolving case law and DOJ guidance; if Circle Care contracts with state Medicaid programs or public entities, Title II web rules with WCAG 2.1 AA may apply via contract.
  • Plan: WCAG 2.2 AA as the bar; automated (axe-core) plus manual screen reader testing (VoiceOver, TalkBack) and testing with older adults. See CC-78.

docs.title: 8. Guardianship / POA document handling
docs.text:
• Documents uploaded as "Legal authority" are reviewed by the internal review team (/app/review, CC-24). Reviewers see only the legal document queue.
  • Questions: what does a reviewer actually need to confirm (name match, signature, court seal, activation/springing conditions, expiration, scope — healthcare vs. financial)? What liability arises if a reviewer approves a forged or revoked document?
  • Retention: legal documents are highly sensitive; keep only as long as needed to evidence the verification decision (Q10).
  • Scope limits: a healthcare POA may not authorize everything in the app (e.g., removing family members). Map app permissions to typical authority scope.
  • Product tension to flag: the elder retains rights even with a guardian. Today the policy lets the guardian approve med changes and write settings; the elder is notified of every decision (CC-65) but cannot block them.

docs.title: 9. Other areas to check
docs.text:
• FDA: Circle Care does not diagnose or recommend treatment; medication reminders and adherence logging are generally viewed as low-risk wellness/administrative functions. Confirm no feature crosses into device software (e.g., dose recommendations).
  • Elder abuse mandatory reporting: if the review team or support staff see evidence of abuse, are there reporting obligations? (Q12)
  • COPPA: not expected (no users under 13), but family members could include minors (e.g., grandchildren). Set a minimum age.
  • Electronic signatures / consent records: consent version and timestamp are stored (settings.consent, CC-22), including "on behalf" consent with a documented reason.

docs.title: 10. Payments, SSNs and identity data (added 2026-11-15)
docs.text:
• Why SSNs are collected. Sign-up asks every account for an SSN to verify identity, but nothing verifies it yet: no identity-check vendor is connected, and the app only checks the format and that the SSN isn't on another account. Collecting it for elders, caregivers and guardians alike needs a purpose counsel agrees with. If it is used for caregiver background checks through a vendor, the Fair Credit Reporting Act may apply, with its own consent and adverse-action steps (Q14, Q15).
  • Controls in place today (see the data inventory): SSNs are stored only encrypted, with a separate fingerprint to stop one SSN on two accounts; bank and card numbers go only to the vault and Circle Care keeps a token and the last four; audit records keep the last four only; real values are refused outside production (CC-180 to CC-188).
  • Gaps already in the backlog (from the threat model (CC-10)): no second sign-in step on the server for accounts that hold an SSN and bank details (CC-200); no way to end every session or reset a password (CC-201); a signed-in account can learn whether an SSN is already registered (CC-204); the database connection doesn't verify the server's certificate (CC-203).
  • Who moves the money. "Pay for care by ACH" can mean Circle Care debits the guardian and pays a caregiver or agency. That may make it a money transmitter, or a financial institution under GLBA and the FTC Safeguards Rule, unless a licensed processor holds and moves the funds (Q16). ACH debits need the guardian's authorization under Nacha rules and Regulation E, and recurring card charges may fall under state automatic-renewal laws (Q17).
  • Paying from the elder's money. A guardian or agent under a power of attorney who pays for care from the elder's funds usually has a duty to keep records and account for that spending, and some courts require yearly accountings. Circle Care could help with receipts, but shouldn't suggest it meets a court's rules (Q25).
  • Paying caregivers. If a family pays a private caregiver through Circle Care, tax and worker-classification duties (for example household employment) may arise for the family; Circle Care should not give tax advice. A question for counsel before money moves, not a product promise.

docs.title: 11. Open questions for counsel
docs.text: # Question Q1 Is the public statement "designed to the HIPAA standard… even where HIPAA doesn't legally apply" acceptable, or does it create misleading expectations? Q2 Which home-care agencies are covered entities (e.g., private-pay-only agencies)? How should contracts differ? Q3 In a mixed circle, which data is PHI under a BAA and which is consumer data? Can one data store serve both? Q4 Does the amended HBNR apply in consumer mode? What counts as a "breach of security" for us? Q5 What do we need to meet the MHMDA (policy, consent flows, deletion timelines)? Does it apply if we have no WA users at launch? Q6 Does door check-in location capture create "precise location" or geofencing issues under state laws? Q7 Do CMIA and CCPA/CPRA apply at our expected size? Q8 Who may consent to SMS on an elder's behalf (guardian, POA)? Q9 Is our SOS feature at risk of being perceived as a monitored emergency service? What disclaimers are needed? Q10 Minimum and maximum retention for legal authority documents and audit logs (currently 6 years — RETENTION_YEARS). Q11 Liability allocation if guardian verification is wrong; insurance needs. Q12 Any reporting obligations when staff see signs of elder abuse or neglect? Q13 Elder's right of access: guardian-only notes (notes.private) are hidden from the elder by policy. Is that permissible where HIPAA applies? Q14 Do we need an SSN from every account at all, and for what purpose? Which state SSN laws apply (published SSN privacy policy, limits on display and transmission), and could identity be verified without one? Q15 If SSNs are used for caregiver background checks or identity checks through a vendor, does the FCRA apply, and what consent and adverse-action steps are needed? Q16 Does holding guardians' bank and card details, or moving money for care, make Circle Care a financial institution under GLBA and the FTC Safeguards Rule, or a money transmitter under state law and FinCEN rules? Does using a licensed processor that holds the funds avoid that? Q17 What ACH authorization (Nacha rules, Regulation E) and card terms do we need, do state automatic-renewal laws apply to recurring charges, and is "no platform fee" a safe public claim? Q18 Is a profile photo PHI in the agency model? Would any later face matching bring in state biometric laws, and what consent would that need? Q19 Family chat: when an agency caregiver is in the chat, which messages are PHI under the BAA? What retention, deletion and legal-hold rules apply to chat, and may a caregiver keep seeing messages after leaving the circle? Q20 Voice replies: is sending a member's voice to a browser speech service a disclosure that needs a BAA (agency) or consent (consumer, MHMDA), or a breach under the HBNR? Should voice be off by default or processed on the device? Q21 The elder can keep daily check-ins private from the guardian. Can a guardian with healthcare authority override that, and must the evening recap respect it? Q22 Which state breach laws do SSNs, financial account numbers and an email with its password trigger, alongside HIPAA and the HBNR, and what notice timelines follow (CC-34)? Q23 With card numbers entered in Stripe's own fields, is Circle Care's PCI DSS scope the smallest self-assessment (SAQ A), and what does it become if card numbers ever pass through our server, as the development vault does today (SAQ D)? Q24 Do state data-security laws such as Massachusetts 201 CMR 17.00 and the New York SHIELD Act apply to us, and what must our written security program include? Q25 When a guardian or agent pays for care from the elder's money through Circle Care, what records must they keep, and should the app help without claiming to meet a court's accounting rules?

docs.text:

docs.title: Data Inventory
docs.text: Notion story: CC-9 Data inventory and classification Status: DRAFT v4, reviewed against main on 2026-11-15 (demo state version 11, the 11 Postgres tables and 2 masked views in server/migrations/001_init.sql, and the schema_migrations log). v3 and v4 follow two Lead Architect review rounds the same day: the access logs are PHI and sensitive, not operational; readable ids are PHI; and the field check reads the database catalog and the live demo data as well as types.ts. v1 was written on 2026-10-19, before Sprints 11 to 13 added accounts, SSNs, bank accounts, cards, profile photos, everyday care and the family chat. Retention and production storage still describe the intended design and need sign-off by the security officer and counsel (CC-8, CC-79). All people in the prototype are fictional.

docs.title: How this inventory stays true
docs.text:
The classes live in code, in src/data/classification.ts. A unit test, src/__tests__/classification.test.ts, fails, naming the field, when:

  • a state field in src/data/types.ts has no class, or a classified one no longer exists. The reader refuses any declaration or field shape it can't parse (an object inside a union, say) instead of skipping it, and checks its own count of fields;
  • a field in the live demo data (seed(), after the alert rules run) has no class. This second check doesn't depend on reading types.ts;
  • a column has no class. The test runs every migration on an in-memory Postgres and lists, from Postgres's own catalog, the columns of every table, view, materialized view and foreign table in every schema, so it sees what the database has, however the SQL was written;
  • a record that holds PHI tags who or when as anything but PHI (see the rules below);
  • this document's field tables (below) list a field under a different class than the code, or list an entity twice.

So a new field can't reach main without a class here. Re-run the review, and update the status line, whenever a story adds data.

docs.title: Classification key
docs.text:
Class Meaning Handling PHI Health information about Maggie, or something that reveals it (a medicine, a dose, a care task, a visit, a feeling). Legally PHI only where HIPAA applies (CC-8); treated as PHI everywhere by design, and as consumer health data under state laws. Encrypted at rest and in transit; role-checked by can() (CC-18/19); never in lock-screen text, email, SMS, server or debug logs, or analytics. The circle's access log can name medicines and documents, so it is protected as PHI PII Identifies a person but says nothing about health on its own: names, phone, email, photo, relationship Encrypted; owner or circle only; not in analytics Sensitive financial or identity SSNs, bank and card details, payment tokens, password hashes Never stored in plain text: SSNs only as ciphertext, bank and card numbers only as a vault token and last four; never returned in full by the API; writes audit-logged with last four only; real values refused outside production (CC-182) Operational Ids, timestamps, settings and flags needed to run the service May appear in security logs by id only

Two rules keep the tags consistent, and the test checks both:

  • Who and when go with the record. In a record that holds PHI, the member who did it and the time are PHI too, because together they say who cared for Maggie, and when. Each nested object counts as its own record, and a link to another record doesn't make it one, so the chat's read times stay operational though its messages are PHI. This rule doesn't by itself make an id, a status or a flag PHI. The test goes by field name (by, at, …By, …At and a short list of member references), so new who or when fields should follow that naming.
  • Demo ids are readable. They embed what they are about: med-lisinopril, t-bath, ap-metformin, s-ana for a caregiver's shift, appt-auto-med-lisinopril-… for an automatic refill, and b- plus the count time for a bottle. So Medication.id, CareTask.id, Approval.id, Shift.id, Appointment.id, MedSupply.bottleId, the fields that hold those ids and alert keys built from them are PHI. Production should use opaque ids.

"Who can see" names the permission-matrix resource (MATRIX in src/data/policy.ts, rendered in the permission matrix) and the roles that may read it. pro@shift is a paid caregiver while checked in to a visit. When Maggie pauses sharing (CC-81), family and paid caregivers keep only sos, emergencyCard and circle.

docs.title: Retention and deletion (intended)
docs.text:
• Close the circle (elder or guardian, data.delete): the prototype wipes circle state, destroys the device key and clears the file store (wipeDevice, CC-33), so any leftover copy is unreadable. Saving is paused during the wipe and any save already under way is dropped, so it can't write the circle back (CC-195). Production: delete within 30 days (as /privacy promises), including backups on their normal rotation.
  • Delete an account: persona, session, photo, fingerprint, vault token, bank and card rows go with the users row (ON DELETE CASCADE). audit_events has no foreign key, so it keeps the masked history. There is no account-deletion endpoint yet, so today this happens only by deleting the row directly. Confirm the design with counsel.
  • Audit logs: at least 6 years (RETENTION_YEARS = 6 in src/data/audit.ts). The circle's access log names medicines and documents (PHI) and the server log keeps last fours (sensitive), so both are protected like the data they describe. Confirm with counsel (CC-8 Q10).
  • Sessions: expire after 12 hours, but nothing purges expired rows yet: each is deleted only when its cookie comes back, on sign-out, or on a lock-out at the password check before an SSN change (a sign-in lock-out leaves existing sessions in place). A purge job is needed before production.
  • Member removed or time limit ends (CC-25): access stops at once; what they wrote stays with the circle as part of Maggie's care record.

docs.title: Vendor and BAA Register
docs.text: Notion story: CC-30 Vendor BAA register Status: TEMPLATE — no vendors selected, no contracts or BAAs signed. Every row needs an owner. Not legal advice; BAA requirements to be confirmed by counsel (CC-8).

docs.title: Rules for this register
docs.text:
1. Default to PHI-free. For every vendor, first ask: can we design so this vendor never receives PHI? If yes, document the design control and verify it in testing. If no, a signed BAA is required before any production data flows.
  2. A BAA is necessary but not sufficient: also review the vendor's security posture (SOC 2 Type II / HITRUST report, encryption, breach notice terms, subprocessors, data location, deletion on termination).
  3. Free tiers and consumer plans of most vendors do not include BAAs. Confirm the specific plan.
  4. Even where HIPAA does not apply (consumer mode), keep the same controls; the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule and state laws treat unauthorized sharing as a breach.
  5. Review each row at least yearly and whenever the vendor's use changes.

docs.title: HIPAA Security Risk Analysis
docs.text: Notion story: CC-79 HIPAA security risk analysis Status: Draft — requires review by a designated security officer. No security officer has been designated yet. Prepared by the product owner on 2026-10-19 against the planned MVP; the prototype holds fictional data only. Not legal advice. Structure follows the HHS Security Risk Assessment (SRA) approach: scope → assets → threats/vulnerabilities → current controls → likelihood × impact → risk rating → treatment.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
• ePHI in scope: all circle data classified PHI in CC-9 (medications, doses, tasks, visits, hand-offs, notes, documents, SOS events, check-ins, emergency card, approvals with med changes, alert details).
  • Systems: client apps, API/policy engine, auth/MFA, database, object storage, rules/escalation worker, notification providers, review console, backups, staff laptops, pilot research store (should hold no ePHI — verify).
  • People: engineering, support, review team, pilot team.
  • Applicability: HIPAA applies directly only in business-associate scenarios (CC-8). This analysis is done for all circles as the design standard.

docs.title: 3. Scoring method
docs.text:
• Likelihood: 1 Rare · 2 Unlikely · 3 Possible · 4 Likely · 5 Almost certain
  • Impact: 1 Negligible · 2 Minor (one circle, low sensitivity) · 3 Moderate (one circle, PHI exposed or safety feature delayed) · 4 Major (many circles, or harm to an elder) · 5 Severe (platform-wide exposure or safety failure)
  • Risk = L × I: 1–4 Low · 5–9 Medium · 10–16 High · 20–25 Critical
  • Scores are inherent with planned controls (production design) and are preliminary estimates by the product owner, not measured.

docs.title: Pilot Plan
docs.text: Notion story: CC-74 Run a pilot with 15–25 care circles Status: DRAFT plan — pilot not started; no circles recruited. Proposed start May 2027 (as stated on the /pilot page). Blocked on production readiness items listed in §9.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Learn, with real families over 8 weeks, whether Circle Care increases verified care tasks completed on time (North Star, CC-6) without making the elder feel watched, and whether caregivers and guardians would keep using it.

The pilot is a learning exercise, not a launch. We expect to find things that don't work.

docs.title: 2. Pilot size and mix
docs.text:
• 15–25 care circles. Below 15, per-persona NPS cohorts will often fall under the minimum of 5 and be hidden on the dashboard.
  • Target mix:
  • at least 8 circles with a professional caregiver visiting (to test shift mode);
  • at least 5 circles with a long-distance guardian;
  • at least 3 states (state-law differences, CC-8);
  • elders with a range of phone comfort.

docs.title: 3. Eligibility
docs.text: Criterion Rule Elder 65+, lives at home or with family, able to give her own consent to join (no proxy consent for the pilot in v1) Guardian / POA Holds healthcare POA or guardianship; willing to upload documents for review (CC-24) Circle At least 2 members besides the elder Devices Elder has an iPhone or Android phone, or a tablet at home; others have smartphones Medicines Elder takes 2+ scheduled medicines Exclusions Hospice or end-of-life care; elder in a facility; anyone employed by a competing product; circles currently in a crisis (recent hospitalization within 2 weeks) — invite later Agencies If an agency caregiver joins, written agency permission; if the agency is a HIPAA covered entity, a BAA must be in place first (CC-8, CC-30)

docs.title: 4. Recruiting via /pilot
docs.text:
• The /pilot page form asks: name, email or phone, role, state, whether a professional caregiver visits, and consent to be contacted. It warns "Please don't include any health information here."
  • In the prototype, only role, state and hasPro are stored (addPilotLead in src/lib/pilot.ts); name and contact are dropped. Production must store contact details in a separate, access-restricted store so we can call people back — and delete them after the pilot.
  • The page promises "We'll reach out within two weeks." Assign an owner to keep that promise.
  • Additional channels: the CC-1 channels (AAAs, senior centers, agencies, support groups); interview participants who opted in.
  • Screening call (15 min) using a short version of the CC-1 screener.

docs.title: 5. Onboarding — white-glove setup call (CC-75)
docs.text:
30-minute call per circle, elder present.

  1. Introductions; explain what the pilot is and isn't (not an emergency monitoring service).
  2. Consent: walk through plain-language consent with read-aloud (CC-22); elder consents herself.
  3. Create the circle; invite members by role; set time-bound access for respite caregivers (CC-25).
  4. Guardian uploads legal document; explain review time.
  5. Enter medicines with the guardian; mark high-priority medicines.
  6. Set check-in window, escalation order, quiet hours.
  7. Elder: choose text size and contrast; try What's next, SOS hold-and-cancel, Call my person.
  8. Show the Privacy Center: who can see, access log, Pause sharing.
  9. Agree on support contact and what to do in a real emergency (call 911 first).

In-app: first-run tour per persona and a "request a setup call" option (settings.setupCallRequested, CC-75).

docs.title: 6. Timeline (8 weeks)
docs.text:
Week Activity −4 to −1 Recruit, screen, schedule setup calls; production readiness gate (§9) 0 Setup calls; baseline survey (how many check-in calls per day today, time spent coordinating) 1 Day-3 check-in call (short); fix onboarding issues 2–3 Normal use; monitor dashboard weekly 4 Mid-point check-in (15 min per persona); in-app NPS prompt 5–7 Normal use; targeted interviews on emerging themes 8 Final conversation (30 min); final NPS; exit survey +2 Synthesis; go/no-go recommendation

Matches the /pilot page promise: "A 30-minute setup call, two short check-ins, and a final conversation."

docs.title: 7. Success metrics
docs.text:
Viewed on the internal pilot dashboard /app/pilot (CC-77). The prototype dashboard currently shows a "Sample cohort" of invented numbers to design the layout — not results.

Metric Definition Target Source North Star Verified care tasks completed on time per circle per week (median) Rising week over week; baseline set in weeks 1–2 Dose and task logs Dose confirmation rate Scheduled doses with a taken/skipped/refused record ÷ scheduled doses ≥90% (dashboard goal) doses Daily check-in rate Days with an "I'm OK" in the window ÷ pilot days ≥80% by week 8 checkins Alert answered time Median minutes from critical/warning alert to acknowledgment <10 min median Alerts, SOS acknowledgments NPS by persona % 9–10 minus % 0–6, per elder / caregiver / guardian Report only where n ≥ 5 (MIN_COHORT); targets set after baseline In-app feedback (CC-76) Weekly active circles Circles with any activity in the week ≥80% of enrolled through week 8 Aggregates Guardrails Sharing paused 7+ days; members removed; alert volume per guardian per week Watch and follow up, no target Aggregates

Qualitative: did the elder feel more or less in control? Did caregivers save time? Did guardians call less?

docs.title: 8. Consent and data handling
docs.text:
• Pilot data is separate from circle data (src/lib/pilot.ts pattern): pilot leads and NPS responses live in their own store with no link to circle records.
  • De-identified: dashboard shows aggregates only; groups under 5 hidden; free-text feedback scrubbed of health terms (scrubHealth) and never shown on the dashboard.
  • Deletion: pilot research data is deleted 12 months after the pilot ends (stated on the dashboard). Circle data follows normal product rules: a family that leaves can close the circle and have data deleted (the /pilot page says "Your data is deleted when you do").
  • Interview notes follow CC-1 de-identification rules.
  • No data used for anything other than improving Circle Care; no sale, no advertising.
  • Incentive: free for life for pilot families plus a thank-you gift card (as promised on /pilot) — budget and legal review of "free for life" needed.

docs.title: 9. Production readiness gate (must be true before week 0)
docs.text:
• [ ] Real backend with server-side permission checks (CC-19) — currently none.
  • [ ] Real push/SMS delivery with PHI-free content and tested SOS fallback.
  • [ ] BAAs in place for vendors that may touch PHI (CC-30).
  • [ ] HIPAA security risk analysis reviewed (CC-79).
  • [ ] Incident response roles assigned; tabletop run (CC-34).
  • [ ] External pen test completed and highs fixed (CC-78).
  • [ ] Counsel reviewed consent text, privacy policy, pilot terms (CC-8).

docs.title: 10. Exit criteria
docs.text:
Continue to broader beta if all are true: - Dose confirmation ≥90% in weeks 5–8 for most circles. - Median alert answered under 10 minutes. - At least 70% of circles still active in week 8. - No SEV-1 incidents; any SEV-2 resolved with root cause fixed. - Elders, in final conversations, mostly report feeling in control (qualitative).

Stop or rethink if any is true: - A safety failure (SOS or escalation not delivered) that we can't explain and fix. - Elders report feeling surveilled in a majority of circles. - Caregivers report net added time in a majority of circles.

Participant exit at any time: circle closed and data deleted on request; NPS responses already given stay de-identified in the research store until its deletion date — disclose this in consent.

docs.title: 11. Human actions
docs.text:
• [ ] Assign pilot owner and support contact.
  • [ ] Production readiness gate (§9).
  • [ ] Budget for incentives and setup-call time.
  • [ ] Counsel review of consent and "free for life" promise.

docs.title: Recruiting Plan and Screener
docs.text:
Notion story: CC-1 Recruit and screen interview participants · CC-197 update the kit for the built features Status: DRAFT v2 / TEMPLATE, updated 2026-11-15 (CC-197). No participants have been recruited or contacted. Every step below needs a human to run it.

Circle Care is a CSPO-training concept product. This plan describes how discovery interviews would be run. Nothing here reports real research.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
Recruit enough people across the three personas to test whether the core problems Circle Care is built around are real, frequent and painful:

  • Elders (like Margaret "Maggie" Lee): staying independent while accepting help, and keeping control over who knows what.
  • Professional caregivers (like Ana Rivera): proving work was done, and hand-offs between shifts.
  • Legal guardians / healthcare POA holders (like Sarah Lee): knowing Mom is OK without calling five times a day, and making decisions with good information.

Secondary: family helpers (like grandson James) and respite caregivers (like Ruth Okafor). Interview 1–2 of each if they come up naturally, but they do not count toward quotas.

docs.title: 2. Quotas
docs.text:
Segment Minimum Stretch Mix to aim for Elders (70+, living at home) 6 8 At least 2 living alone; at least 2 who use a smartphone only for calls/texts; at least 1 with low vision or hearing Professional caregivers 6 8 At least 3 agency-employed, at least 2 private-pay/independent; at least 2 non-native English speakers Legal guardians / POA holders 5 7 At least 2 long-distance (more than 1 hour away); at least 1 court-appointed guardian (not POA); at least 1 who also works full time Family helpers (bonus) 0 2 —

Stop recruiting a segment when two consecutive interviews produce no new themes (saturation), but never below the minimum.

Where possible, recruit linked triads (an elder, their caregiver and their guardian) — at least 2 triads — so we can compare how each person describes the same situation. Interview each person separately.

docs.title: 3. Recruiting channels
docs.text: Channel Reaches How to approach Owner Notes Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) Elders, family caregivers Email the outreach coordinator; offer a 1-page summary and the consent outline; ask to post a flyer or mention in newsletter TBD Do not ask the agency to share client contact details. Participants contact us. Senior centers Elders Ask to host a 20-minute "tell us about your day" table; leave flyers with tear-off contact tabs TBD Print flyer at 16pt+ font. Home-care agencies Professional caregivers, agency managers Ask the owner/manager for permission to post in the break room or staff chat TBD Make clear the agency will not see individual answers. Avoid recruiting through supervisors present in the room. Caregiver support groups (in person and online) Guardians, family Ask the facilitator first; post only where rules allow TBD Respect group norms; no cold DMs. Elder-law attorneys / guardianship associations Court-appointed guardians Ask to share a flyer with clients TBD Optional; slower channel. Personal network (2nd-degree only) All Ask friends to forward, never interview close friends or family TBD Cap at 30% of any segment to avoid bias. /pilot page in the prototype All Later-stage only (see CC-74) TBD Collects role/state only.

docs.title: 4. Screener
docs.text:
Ask by phone or a short form. Read questions aloud for elders. Record answers in the tracker using a participant ID only.

What we keep from screening. The participant ID, segment, state and the answers marked record for mix, in the tracker (§8). Record E4 as a number and E6 as a category (eyesight, hearing, hands), never the reason or a condition. Contact details for people who don't qualify are deleted the same day; for people who do, they go only in the ID key (§7). Read this at the end of the call: "We keep your answers under a number, not your name. We don't need to know about your health, and if you tell us something we don't need, we won't write it down."

docs.title: 4.1 All segments
docs.text:
1. Which best describes you? (Older adult who gets some help at home / Paid caregiver / Legal guardian or power of attorney for an older adult / Family member who helps / Other) — route to segment
  2. What state do you live in? — aim for at least 3 states
  3. Are you, or anyone in your household, employed by a company that makes health or caregiving apps? — exclude if yes
  4. Have you taken part in a paid research interview in the last 6 months? — exclude if 2+
  5. Are you comfortable with a conversation of up to 70 minutes, with breaks, by phone, video or in person? Which do you prefer?

docs.title: 4.2 Elders
docs.text: # Question Qualify if E1 How old are you? 70+ (65–69 OK if receiving regular help) E2 Where do you live? (own home, with family, assisted living, nursing home) Own home or with family E3 Does anyone help you with things like medicines, meals, appointments or errands? How often? At least weekly E4 How many medicines do you take on a regular schedule? 2+ E5 What kind of phone do you use, and what do you use it for? Any (record for mix) E6 Is there anything that makes phone screens or calls harder for you? (eyesight, hearing, hands) Any (record for mix) E7 Are you able to agree to take part yourself today? Yes — if the person cannot give their own consent, do not interview them

docs.title: 4.3 Professional caregivers
docs.text: # Question Qualify if C1 Do you currently provide paid in-home care to an older adult? Yes C2 Through an agency, privately, or both? Record for mix C3 How many clients do you see in a typical week? 1+ C4 Do you help with medicines (reminding, handing, or administering)? Yes for 4+ of the 6 C5 How do you currently record what you did on a visit? (paper, agency app, texts, nothing) Any C6 Would your employer need to approve your taking part? If yes, recruit only with written agency OK

docs.title: 4.4 Legal guardians / POA holders
docs.text: # Question Qualify if G1 Do you hold healthcare power of attorney or a court guardianship for an older adult? Yes (record which) G2 Is the document currently in effect (activated)? Record — both OK G3 How far do you live from them? Record for mix G4 Who else helps care for them? At least one other person (family or paid) G5 In the last month, how often did you worry you didn't know whether they were OK? Record (do not lead)

docs.title: 5. Consent form outline (needs review before use)
docs.text:
Plain language, 14pt+ print, read aloud for elders. Draft sections:

  1. Who we are and that Circle Care is a student/concept project, not a company selling anything.
  2. What we will ask about (daily routines, help, privacy), that we will show a practice app, and how long it takes.
  3. Taking part is voluntary; you can skip any question or stop at any time and still receive the incentive.
  4. Recording: audio only, with separate opt-in; notes taken either way.
  5. Health details. We ask about your daily routine and the help you get. We may ask how many medicines you take on a schedule and whether eyesight, hearing or your hands make phones harder, but never which conditions you have or what your medicines are. We record no health details beyond what you choose to tell us. Please do not tell us specific diagnoses, medicine names or doctors' names. If you do, we replace them in the notes and the transcript with "[condition]" or "[med]". If you are a caregiver or guardian, the same goes for the person you care for.
  6. The practice app. It shows made-up people (Maggie, Sarah, James, Ana and Ruth), not you or anyone you know. Please don't type or say anything real into it. It runs on our research phone, not yours. After every session we reset the practice app and clear the phone's browser data for it, so what you tapped or typed isn't kept. Its microphone is switched off for the chat, so you type, or tell us what to type.
  7. How notes are stored. Notes use your participant number, never your name. They are kept in an encrypted folder that only the research team can open, and never pasted into tools that learn from what is typed into them. Recordings are transcribed by the team, or by a tool that doesn't learn from what it is given, and names are taken out of the transcript. The list that links your name to your number is kept separately, in one locked file.
  8. When things are deleted. Recordings within 30 days of transcription; until then the recording still has your voice and anything you said. The name-to-number list once your incentive is paid and any follow-up is done. De-identified notes within 12 months. You can ask us to delete your notes and recording sooner, any time until the name-to-number list is deleted. After that we can no longer tell which notes are yours.
  9. Quotes may be used without names or identifying details.
  10. Contact for questions or withdrawal.
  11. Signature or recorded verbal consent with date.

Human action: have the consent text reviewed (e.g., by an instructor or IRB-style reviewer) before first use. Elders who cannot consent for themselves are excluded; we do not take proxy consent for research.

docs.title: 6. Incentive
docs.text:
• Proposed: $40 gift card for the main session (up to 70 minutes); $20 for a 15-minute follow-up.
  • Offer the choice of a physical card mailed or e-card; some elders will not want an e-card.
  • Budget for minimum quotas: 17 × $40 = $680 (+ 20% buffer). Funding not yet secured.

docs.title: 7. De-identification rules
docs.text:
• Assign IDs at screening: E01…, C01…, G01…, F01…; triads share a suffix (e.g., E03-T1, C02-T1, G04-T1).
  • Keep the name ↔ ID key in one access-restricted file, separate from notes. Delete it after incentives are paid and follow-ups are done.
  • In notes: replace names with role words ("my daughter", "the aide"); replace medicine names with "[med]"; replace conditions with "[condition]"; replace employer/agency names with "[agency]"; generalize location to state.
  • Never paste notes into tools that train on inputs.
  • Recordings: store encrypted, delete within 30 days after transcription.
  • Notes: one file per participant ID in the encrypted research folder. Delete the de-identified notes within 12 months, and log each deletion (date and ID only) in the tracker.
  • The practice app: run sessions on a research phone, never the participant's, in a guest browser profile, with keyboard learning and suggestions turned off and the microphone blocked for the prototype site. After each session, open the presenter sheet and tap Reset demo so no taps, typed chat messages or check-ins carry over, then clear the browser's site data and history for the prototype. Reset demo resets the practice app only: feedback answers, pilot sign-ups and browser history are cleared by the site-data step.

docs.title: 8. Scheduling tracker (template)
docs.text: ID Segment Channel Screened (date) Qualifies? Consent sent Session date/time Mode Interviewer Note-taker Incentive sent Follow-up? Notes (no PII) E01 Elder E02 Elder C01 Caregiver G01 Guardian

docs.title: 9. Human actions before starting
docs.text:
None of these can be done by the product team's agents. Each needs a named person.

  • [ ] Recruiting: name an owner for each channel and start recruiting (CC-1).
  • [ ] Incentives: secure the incentive budget, and decide whether the longer sessions in the v2 guides (up to 70 minutes) change the amount.
  • [ ] Consent review: get the consent text in §5 reviewed before first use.
  • [ ] Safety protocol: write the protocol for disclosures of harm (see the elder guide).
  • [ ] Agency approvals: get written agency OK for caregivers who need it (C6).
  • [ ] Interpreter: decide the interpreter budget for caregivers who prefer another language.
  • [ ] Print large-type flyers.
  • [ ] Set up encrypted storage for recordings, notes and the ID key.
  • [ ] Set up a research phone: a guest browser profile, keyboard learning off, the microphone blocked for the prototype site, and a check that Reset demo and clearing site data work on it.

docs.title: Interview Guide — Elders
docs.text:
Notion story: CC-2 Interview guide: elders · CC-197 concept tests of the built features Status: DRAFT v2, updated 2026-11-15 (CC-197). Not yet piloted or used. No interviews have taken place.

Participants come through the CC-1 screener. Only interview people who can give their own consent. Session length up to 70 minutes: §1 to §6 take about 54, §6b 10 and the wrap-up 3. Offer breaks. If the session reaches 55 minutes before §6b, or the person tires, move §6b to the 15-minute follow-up.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Understand a typical day: what help arrives, from whom, and how the person feels about it.
  2. Learn how medicines are managed today and where it goes wrong.
  3. Understand what independence, dignity and control mean to this person in concrete terms — what they would and would not want others to know.
  4. Learn what they do when something goes wrong (a fall, feeling unwell, a missed visit).
  5. React to three prototype tasks: the three-button home, confirming a dose, and the Privacy Center.
  6. React to the everyday features built since October: the My day check-ins, the family chat, and what Sarah sees in her evening recap and refill alerts.

docs.title: Interviewer reminders
docs.text:
• Sit at eye level, face the person, speak clearly but do not talk down. Use their preferred name.
  • Ask about past behavior, not hypotheticals ("Tell me about the last time…").
  • Do not correct or teach. If they struggle with the prototype, that is data.
  • If they mention a diagnosis or medicine name, do not write it down; note "[condition]" / "[med]".
  • If they disclose risk of harm (neglect, abuse, an unsafe situation), pause the interview and follow the safety protocol agreed with the research lead before fieldwork starts (human action: write this protocol).
  • Run the concept tests on the research phone, never the participant's. After the session, tap Reset demo in the presenter sheet so nothing carries over to the next person.
  • Chat voice: before the session, block the microphone for the prototype site in the research phone's browser (screener §9), so the chat opens its typing box instead of listening. In Chrome and most browsers the chat's voice reply sends speech to an online service, though the screen says it stays on the device (CC-222), and one tap starts it listening to the whole room. Ask what they expect happens to their words if they spoke. Remove this line once CC-222 is done.
  • The dose voice in §6 T2 runs only on the device, so it is safe. Where the browser can't do that, tapping Answer with my voice says voice answers aren't available on this device; with the microphone blocked, tapping it shows Voice isn't working right now. Please tap a button instead. Both are expected: note them under T2's "tries voice?".
  • The demo's medicine names (Metformin, Lisinopril, Vitamin D3, Atorvastatin) belong to the made-up Maggie and are fine in prompts. Never note them as the participant's.

docs.title: 1. Warm-up (5 min)
docs.text:
• Thank you for having me. How long have you lived here?
  • What does a good day look like for you?
  • Who are the people you see or talk to most in a week?

docs.title: 2. Daily life and help (10 min)
docs.text:
• Walk me through yesterday from when you woke up.
  • Who helps you with anything? What do they help with?
  • How did that help start? Whose idea was it?
  • What do you still do entirely on your own that matters to you?
  • Is there anything people help with that you'd rather do yourself?

docs.title: 3. Medicines (8 min)
docs.text:
• How do you keep track of your medicines today? (pill box, alarm, someone reminds you)
  • Tell me about the last time a dose was missed or taken twice. What happened? Who found out?
  • When someone reminds you about medicine, how does it feel? Does it depend on who reminds you?
  • If you decide to skip a dose on purpose, who should know? Who should not?

docs.title: 4. Independence, dignity and control (12 min) — core
docs.text:
• When your daughter/son or a caregiver checks on you, how does that feel?
  • Has anyone ever known something about you that you wish they hadn't? How did they find out?
  • If you could decide exactly who sees what — medicines, notes from the aide, your appointments — how would you split it?
  • Is there anything you'd want only your [guardian/daughter] to see, and not the aide? Anything the other way around?
  • If you could switch off everyone's view for a while, would you ever use that? When?
  • Has anyone ever made a decision about your care without asking you? Tell me about it.
  • What would make you feel "checked up on" versus "looked after"?

Probe: "You said ___. Can you tell me more about that?" / "What made that feel that way?"

docs.title: 5. When something goes wrong (7 min)
docs.text:
• Tell me about the last time you needed help quickly. What did you do?
  • Do you have a button, pendant or phone setting for emergencies? Do you wear/use it? Why or why not?
  • Who do you want called first? Does that change at night?
  • How do you feel about a daily "I'm OK" tap each morning? (Ask after exploring how people check on them today.)

docs.title: 6. Concept test — prototype tasks (12 min)
docs.text:
Use the prototype at /#/app → Maggie, on a phone held by the participant. Set text size to their preference first. Read each task aloud; do not demonstrate.

Task Prompt Watch for Success = T1 Three-button home "This is a phone app. What do you think you can do here?" Does the person read all three buttons? Do they fear pressing SOS by accident? Names at least 2 of the 3 actions without help T2 Confirm a dose "It's time for your morning tablet. Show me how you'd tell the app you took it." Then: "Now imagine you decided not to take it." Finds "What's next"; finds taken/skipped/refused; reaction to the word "refused"; tries voice? Records "taken" and a non-taken status unaided T3 Privacy Center "You'd like to see who can look at your information." Then: "Now you want a break from sharing." Understands the list of people; reaction to the access log; finds Pause sharing; understands SOS still works Finds the list and pause switch; explains in own words what pause does T4 Hold SOS (optional) "Show me what you'd do if you fell and needed help." Is the 2-second hold discoverable? Is the 10-second cancel reassuring or stressful? Starts SOS and cancels unaided

After each task: "On a scale of 1 to 5, how easy was that?" and "What would you change?"

Close the concept test with: "Who in your life would you want in a circle like this? Who would you leave out?"

Before §6b, turn Pause sharing back off: T3 leaves it on. Any My day tap while sharing is paused makes that day private, so T5's footer and T8's Her day would show it as private. If that happens, tap Reset demo, sign in as Maggie again and set their text size again.

docs.title: 6b. Concept test — everyday care built since October (10 min)
docs.text:
Same phone, still as Maggie. For T8, switch to Sarah in the presenter sheet (Demo mode), so her screens show what the participant just did, then hand the phone back. If they turned check-in sharing off in T6, ask whether to turn it back on before T8. If they keep it off, Her day shows as private, and their reaction to that is part of the test.

Task Prompt Watch for Success = T5 My day "This card is for how your day is going. Show me how you'd say you feel good and had two glasses of water." Then: "You've had breakfast too." Finds the card under the three big buttons; expects a Submit button; reads the line saying Sarah can see this; un-ticks by mistake? Records a feeling, water and a meal unaided T6 Keep it to yourself "Say you'd rather Sarah didn't see how you feel for a while." Finds Share daily check-ins with Sarah in My privacy. Then probe: "Sarah gets a note when you change this. How do you feel about that?" Finds the switch and explains in own words what Sarah would see T7 Family chat "Send Sarah a message asking her to visit on Sunday." (The microphone is blocked; if typing is hard for them, type what they dictate.) Finds the chat tile and Open chat; reads who can see the chat; expects the aide to see it?; what they expect the microphone to do Finds the chat, gets the message sent (typed or dictated), and names who can read it T8 What Sarah sees (optional) As Sarah, after Skip to 7 PM for the evening recap (the card already shows after 6 PM): "Each evening Sarah sees this about your day. She and the aide also get a note when your pills are running low." What feels fine, what feels like too much; notices Her day shows only what they share; reaction to the refill note Says, in their own words, what they'd keep and what they'd change

After each task: "On a scale of 1 to 5, how easy was that?" For T8 ask instead: "How do you feel about Sarah seeing this?"

docs.title: 7. Wrap-up (3 min)
docs.text:
• Is there anything about getting help at home that I should have asked and didn't?
  • Would you be open to a 15-minute follow-up?
  • Confirm incentive delivery. Thank them.

docs.title: Interview Guide — Professional Caregivers
docs.text:
Notion story: CC-3 Interview guide: professional caregivers · CC-197 concept tests of the built features Status: DRAFT v2, updated 2026-11-15 (CC-197). Not yet piloted or used. No interviews have taken place.

Participants come through the CC-1 screener. If the caregiver works for an agency and the agency required approval, confirm written approval is on file. Never ask for client names. Session length up to 70 minutes; schedule around shifts and offer evenings. If time is short, drop T4. Run sessions Monday to Saturday, when the demo gives Ana a shift.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Understand a real shift end to end: arrival, tasks, medicines, documentation, leaving.
  2. Measure the workload of documentation and communication today (tools, duplicate entry, time spent).
  3. Understand how caregivers prove work was done (verification) and how they feel about being checked.
  4. Understand hand-offs between caregivers and to family/guardians.
  5. React to three prototype tasks: shift check-in, giving a dose, and end-of-shift hand-off.
  6. React to the everyday features built since October: pills on hand and refills, the family chat, and what the family sees from Maggie's check-ins and Sarah's evening recap.

docs.title: Interviewer reminders
docs.text:
• Caregivers may worry this is an evaluation. Say clearly: "We are not checking your work, and your employer will not see what you say."
  • Ask about the last shift, not shifts in general.
  • No client names, no medicine names, no addresses. Use "[client]", "[med]".
  • Respect language preference; offer an interpreter if needed (budget TBD).
  • Run the concept tests on the research phone, never the participant's. After the session, tap Reset demo in the presenter sheet so nothing carries over to the next person.
  • Chat voice: before the session, block the microphone for the prototype site in the research phone's browser (screener §9), so the chat opens its typing box instead of listening. In Chrome and most browsers the chat's voice reply sends speech to an online service, though the screen says it stays on the device (CC-222), and one tap starts it listening to the whole room. Ask what they expect happens to their words if they spoke. Remove this line once CC-222 is done.
  • The demo's medicine names (Metformin, Lisinopril, Vitamin D3, Atorvastatin) belong to the made-up Maggie and are fine in prompts. Never note them as the participant's.

docs.title: 1. Warm-up (5 min)
docs.text:
• How long have you been a caregiver? What got you into it?
  • What kind of clients do you usually work with?
  • What's the best part of the job? The hardest?

docs.title: 2. The last shift (12 min)
docs.text:
• Walk me through your last shift from when you arrived at the door.
  • How did you know what you needed to do that day?
  • What did you write down or record? Where? When — during or after?
  • Did anything not go to plan? What did you do, and who did you tell?
  • How did you leave things for the next person?

docs.title: 3. Workload and tools (10 min) — core
docs.text:
• How many apps, forms or notebooks do you use for one client? Show me if you can (without client details).
  • About how many minutes per shift go to writing things down or texting family?
  • Is any of that unpaid time (before/after the shift)?
  • What do you enter more than once?
  • Which messages from family are useful? Which take time without helping?
  • If you could get rid of one documentation task, what would it be?

Probe on numbers: "Roughly — 5 minutes? 30?" Record their estimate, not ours.

docs.title: 4. Verification and trust (10 min) — core
docs.text:
• How does your agency or the family know you arrived on time? (EVV, GPS app, sign-in sheet, text)
  • How do you feel about location check-in at the door?
  • Has a family ever doubted that something was done? What happened?
  • What would make you feel protected rather than watched?
  • Who should see your notes? Should some notes go only to the guardian?
  • How do you feel about only seeing the client's care plan while you're on shift?

docs.title: 5. Medicines (6 min)
docs.text:
• What exactly do you do with medicines — remind, hand over, open containers, administer?
  • What happens when the client refuses a dose?
  • When a medicine changes, how do you find out? Has that ever gone wrong?

docs.title: 6. Concept test — prototype tasks (12 min)
docs.text:
Use /#/app → Ana on a phone. Read each task aloud. The demo checks Ana in at 8 AM on its own; if she is already on shift, T1 becomes "Show me how you'd know you're on shift."

Run §6b straight after T2, before T3. T3's Send hand-off and check out ends Ana's shift, which hides Pills on hand and the refill buttons and turns off Save as a note, and she can't check in again that day. If T3 has already happened, tap Reset demo, sign in as Ana again and re-add her to the chat.

Task Prompt Watch for Success = T1 Check in "You just arrived at Maggie's. Start your shift." Finds check-in; reaction to plan unlocking only on shift; manual-reason flow Checks in unaided T2 Give a dose "Maggie's morning medicine is due. Record that she took it." Then: "She says no to the evening one." Order of doses; high-priority callout; recording a refusal Records taken + refused T3 Hand-off (run §6b first) "Your shift is over. Leave things for the next person." Reads the auto-drafted summary; edits or accepts; trust in the draft Sends hand-off; says whether they'd trust the draft T4 Shift swap (optional) "You can't make Thursday. Ask someone to cover." Expects the guardian to approve? Finds the flow

After each: "1–5, how easy?" and "Would this save you time or add time compared to today?"

docs.title: 6b. Concept test — everyday care built since October (10 min)
docs.text:
Same phone, still as Ana, on shift from T1 and before T3. Before T6, switch to Sarah in the presenter sheet (Demo mode), open Chat, then People, switch Ana on, and switch back to Ana. The demo keeps its data on this phone only, so a second phone wouldn't add her.

Task Prompt Watch for Success = T5 Pills on hand "One of Maggie's medicines is running low. Which one, and what would you do?" Then: "A new bottle of 30 just arrived." Finds Pills on hand on Today; taps Request refill; the app then says asked Fog City Pharmacy for a refill: do they read that as the app having told the pharmacy? (It only records that Ana asked.) Finds New bottle Names the low medicine, requests a refill and records the new bottle T6 Family chat "Let the family know Maggie enjoyed her walk today." Then: "Tell them she took her Metformin 500 mg with breakfast." (Typed; see the reminder on chat voice.) Reaction to being added by the family; the health-detail check on the second message: Save as a note, Send anyway or Edit; sees only messages from after joining Sends the first message and makes a choice on the check T7 Check-ins and the recap (concept) "Maggie can log how she feels, her water and meals, and only Sarah sees it, when Maggie shares. Sarah also gets an evening recap of Maggie's day at 7 PM." Do they want to see Maggie's check-ins? Why? Would the recap change the texts and calls they get from Sarah? Not scored; record the answers

After T5 and T6: "1–5, how easy?" and "Would this save you time or add time compared to today?"

docs.title: 7. Wrap-up (3 min)
docs.text:
• What would make you not want to use an app like this?
  • Would your agency allow it? Who decides?
  • Follow-up OK? Confirm incentive.

Median self-estimate ≥15 min across 6+ Median under 10 min H-C2 Caregivers re-enter the same information in 2+ places (agency app, family texts, paper). 4+ of 6 2 or fewer H-C3 Door check-in is acceptable when framed as protection against disputes. 4+ of 6 accept it Most see it as surveillance H-C4 An auto-drafted hand-off would be trusted after review and save time. 4+ of 6 would send with minor edits Most would rewrite from scratch H-C5 Shift-limited access to the care plan is acceptable to caregivers. 4+ of 6 Most say they need off-shift access (record why) H-C6 Agency software already covers EVV, so Circle Care must coexist rather than replace it. Agency caregivers describe mandatory EVV tools Few use EVV H-C7 Caregivers would record pill counts and request refills in the app if it saves a call or a text. 4+ of 6 complete T5 and say they'd use it Most say it adds work H-C8 Caregivers understand that Request refill records the request and doesn't contact the pharmacy. Correct means: "it notes that I asked the pharmacy myself; Circle Care doesn't contact it." 4+ of 6 explain it correctly after T5 Most expect the app to have told the pharmacy (the label or the confirmation needs to change) H-C9 Caregivers accept joining the family chat only when the family adds them. 4+ of 6 Most expect to be in it from the start, or not at all H-C10 The health-detail check in the chat feels helpful, not like being policed. 4+ of 6 Most find it intrusive H-C11 Sarah's evening recap would cut the check-up texts caregivers get from family.
