docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. The guardian's command centre. Home answers "Is Mom OK today?" in seconds and lists only the things that need Sarah. Approvals is where medicine changes, new members and shift swaps wait for her decision. Activity is the full history; the Weekly digest is the summary; Settings controls how and when she is alerted.

Why. "I find out about problems days later, from someone else." (guardian hypothesis, CC-4). Remote decision-makers need signal, not noise — and the elder must be able to see what was decided about her.

Business value. Reduces anxiety-driven calls and missed problems; makes the guardian's legal role concrete (approvals) while keeping the elder informed. The digest is the retention loop for family buyers.

docs.title: Home — today at a glance (CC-61)
docs.text:
1. Sarah opens Home: "Good afternoon, Sarah" and a headline that counts what needs her — "Maggie's day is on track.", "One thing needs you." or "3 things need you." — plus the North Star: "68 verified care tasks completed on time."

  2. Seven tiles, each linking to detail:

    Tile Shows Check-in I'm OK 😊 at 8:40 AM · 4-day streak, or Not yet / Missed with the window Medicines Ring 3/3, 3 given, 2 still to come today Tasks 5 of 6 done and the next two open tasks With Maggie now The checked-in caregiver and check-in time, or No one Health Latest heart rate · blood oxygen and N unusual readings today (only while Maggie shares readings) Next appointment Title and Today at 4:30 PM Alerts 4 new — Notifications never show health details

  3. Needs your attention lists, in priority order: an active SOS · late or overdue doses · a missed check-in · a caregiver who hasn't arrived · hand-offs nobody has read (last 3 days) · pending approvals · uncovered shifts this week.

  4. Latest activity shows the six most recent events with See all.
  5. Evening recap (CC-191), from 6 PM: a headline ("A calm day for Maggie.", "1 dose needs a look.", "1 dose is due now.", "Maggie didn't check in today.", "Maggie's check-in is still to come.", "One refill to sort out." or "2 refills to sort out.") and five cells. Medicines gives doses given so far, names each dose not confirmed, skipped or refused with its time and any dose due now, or gives the next dose on a calm day. Check-in gives the time, Not yet while the window is open or Missed after it, and routines done. Visits lists today's caregiver visits. Her day shows Maggie's feeling, water and meals only while she shares them, otherwise Private. Tomorrow shows the first appointment and its prep note, else the first caregiver visit, else Nothing booked. Under it: a refill line for each low medicine (with its Calendar date, or Not on the Calendar yet), Review medicines on a day with a dose that needs a look, a dose due now or a refill, See the week (weekly digest) and a chat chip when there are new messages.
Home on a desktop: status tiles and a short attention list. On phones the side menu becomes a tab bar: Home, Health, Calendar, Approvals and More.

docs.title: Approvals (CC-64, CC-65)
docs.text:
1. Approvals has three parts: a Maggie has a question panel (if she asked one) with Call Maggie; Waiting for you; and Decided.
  2. Each pending request shows its type icon, title, requester and age ("Requested by Ana · 7 hr ago"), the reason, a note box ("Add a note (optional) — Maggie and the requester will see it"), Approve and Decline.
  3. Approve → "Approved — Maggie has been told". The change is applied immediately (medicine schedule, member activated, or shift reassigned).
  4. Decided lists past decisions with the date and note, and a badge Maggie notified or Maggie saw it once she taps OK, got it.
Two pending requests from the demo seed, and one decided request Maggie hasn't opened yet.

docs.title: Activity (CC-62)
docs.text:
1. Activity — "Everything that happened" — groups events by day with filters: Today / 7 days / All and a type menu (Medicines, Tasks, Visits, Hand-offs, Check-ins, Notes, SOS, Approvals).
The chronological activity feed.

docs.title: Weekly digest (CC-83)
docs.text:
1. Maggie's week shows the past 7 days: a ring with the percentage of doses taken (green at 90% or above, orange below), doses taken, caregiver visits completed, check-in streak and the North Star.
  2. Doses taken each day charts daily adherence; days below 90% are highlighted.
  3. Worth knowing lists every dose not taken (with the reason) and any SOS that week.
  4. The email Sarah receives previews the PHI-free email: "Maggie's weekly update is ready. This week: 85% of scheduled items completed, 6 visits, and a 4-day check-in streak. Open Circle Care to see the details." — "To protect Maggie's privacy, this email never includes medicine names, conditions or notes."
Weekly digest. In this capture a notification banner overlaps the date range and the daily bar chart rendered as a narrow column; the numbers are correct.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. A Health section for the guardian with three tabs. Summary highlights today's numbers and any unusual readings. Heart & oxygen charts heart rate and blood oxygen across the day against Maggie's usual range, with every unusual reading explained and a full readings table, plus 30-day weight. Activity shows daily goals, how each hour was spent, steps by hour, last night's sleep stages and a 7-day mood view. Readings arrive every 30 minutes from Maggie's watch — only while Maggie chooses to share them.

Why. Families worry about the hours between visits. A watch already collects useful signals, but raw data is overwhelming and sharing it without the elder's consent is a privacy failure.

Business value. Turns wearable data into a small number of plain-language signals, positions Circle Care for the Release 3 "Insight & Safety" epics, and demonstrates consent-driven sharing of sensitive data.

Not a medical device

Every Health page ends with: "Demo readings are simulated. In the full product they sync from Maggie's watch through Apple Health or Health Connect, only while she chooses to share them. Circle Care isn't a medical device; call 911 in an emergency." Alert thresholds are a guardian preference; the settings page advises "Ask Maggie's doctor what range is right for her."

docs.title: User journey
docs.text:
1. Sarah taps Health (tab bar or side menu). The header reads "From Maggie's watch · new reading every 30 min · last 4:00 PM, next 4:30 PM" with an Alert settings link.
  2. Summary opens with an attention panel — "2 unusual readings today" (e.g. 3:00 AM Blood oxygen low: 89%; 2:30 PM Heart rate high: 128 bpm) and See trend — or "All readings in Maggie's usual range today".
  3. Highlights cards: Heart rate, Blood oxygen (each with a sparkline and today's range), Resting heart rate, Steps, Stand hours, Walking, Sleep last night, State of mind, Weight (30-day change) and Height · BMI. Cards open the relevant tab.
  4. Heart & oxygen shows a day stepper (Today, Yesterday, … up to 6 days back). The heart-rate chart shades the usual range (50–110 bpm) and marks unusual points; the oxygen chart draws an "Alert below 92%" line. Each chart lists its unusual readings with a tag (High, Low, Sudden change).
  5. Show all readings as a table reveals every reading with time, heart rate, oxygen and a note (Asleep or the flag).
  6. Activity shows three goal rings (stand hours, walking minutes, steps), How Maggie spent today so far (one coloured block per hour: sleeping, sitting or resting, standing, walking), Steps by hour, Sleep · night before with stage rows (Awake, REM, Core, Deep) and the 7-hour goal, and Mental well-being · 7 days from her check-in moods, with caregiver visits and mindful minutes.
  7. If Maggie turns sharing off, the page shows "Maggie isn't sharing health readings" — "She can turn this back on in her Privacy Center. Medicines, check-ins, the calendar and SOS work as usual."
Summary: unusual readings first, then highlights. Heart & oxygen: every unusual reading is labelled and explained. Activity, sleep and well-being. The same summary on a phone.

docs.title: Medications & tasks
docs.text: Feature ID / area F-04 · Medication schedule, dose confirmation and care tasks Personas Sarah (manages the plan), Ana (gives and verifies doses, completes tasks), Maggie (takes, skips or refuses), James (family) Status Built in prototype Related stories CC-36 add medication · CC-37 edit / pause · CC-38 caregiver's schedule for today · CC-39 reminder · CC-40 taken / skipped / refused · CC-41 caregiver-verified doses · CC-42 missed-dose escalation timers · CC-43 high-priority medicines · CC-44 recurring care tasks · CC-45 complete tasks with notes · CC-64 change requests via approvals · CC-120 pills on hand · CC-121 low-supply alerts and Calendar refills Last updated 2026-11-14

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. The guardian maintains Maggie's medicines and daily routines. Each dose appears for Maggie as a reminder and for Ana as a checklist item. Every dose ends up taken, skipped or refused — with a name, a time and, when given during a shift, a caregiver-verified mark. Unconfirmed doses escalate: first to the caregiver, then to the guardian, twice as fast for high-priority medicines. Caregivers and family can request changes; only the guardian (or Maggie) changes the plan.

Why. Medication errors are the most common and most dangerous failure in home care. When three people share responsibility, the problem is usually not forgetfulness but not knowing what someone else already did.

Business value. Dose confirmation is the core of the North Star metric. Verified doses give families and agencies evidence of care; escalation reduces the time an unconfirmed dose goes unnoticed.

docs.title: Guardian manages the plan
docs.text:
1. Sarah opens Medications — Medicines & routines. Each medicine card shows a drawing of the pill, name and strength, a High priority or Paused badge, purpose · dose · prescriber, time chips and instructions.
  2. Add medicine opens a form: Name, Strength, Dose, What it's for, Times (add or remove time fields), Instructions, Prescriber, How it looks (shape and colour), and a High priority switch — "Missed doses escalate twice as fast and are marked critical."
  3. Edit opens the same form; Pause / Resume toggles the medicine; History lists every change with who and when (e.g. "times 18:00 → 18:30 (requested by Ana)").
  4. Under Daily routines, Add routine creates a recurring task: What, When, Repeats (Every day / Weekdays / Weekends), Who (Caregiver on shift / Maggie) and an icon.
  5. Every change is logged and appears in Maggie's Updates about me as a decision.
The guardian's medicine list and daily routines.

docs.title: Caregiver gives doses and completes tasks
docs.text:
1. When Ana is checked in, Today with Maggie lists Medicines in time order with a status badge: Later, Due now, Late, Overdue, Given, Skipped, Declined. High-priority medicines carry a red High priority tag.
  2. For an open dose she taps Given (toast "Lisinopril marked as given") or Not given, which asks What happened — Maggie declined or Skipped — and a reason. "Maggie's choice is respected. Sarah will see this in the activity feed."
  3. A dose Maggie recorded herself shows Verify; tapping it marks the dose as caregiver-verified.
  4. The pencil icon opens Request a change to medicine: times (24-hour, comma separated), dose, Pause this medicine, and a required Why? — "Nothing changes until Sarah approves. Maggie will see the decision." → "Sent to Sarah for approval".
  5. Care tasks are checkboxes. The note icon opens a sheet — Note (optional), e.g. "walked 15 minutes, a bit tired" → Mark done ("Sarah and Maggie can see task notes.").
  6. The shift card summarises progress: "3 of 3 doses given this shift".
Ana's checklist. The check-mark after "Given by Ana at 8:06 AM" marks a caregiver-verified dose.

docs.title: Elder answers her reminder
docs.text: 1. Maggie answers from her reminder card — I took it, Skip this time or I don't want to take it (with an optional reason) — or by voice. See Elder experience.

docs.text: 1. Requests appear in Approvals (Guardian dashboard & approvals). On approval, the change is applied to the medicine and recorded in its history; Ana is told and Maggie sees the decision.

docs.title: Refill tracker (CC-120 – CC-121, Sprint 12)
docs.text:
Each medicine can carry a supply: the pill count from the last bottle, when it was counted, pills per dose and the pharmacy (demo: Fog City Pharmacy, fictional).

Rule Detail Pills on hand Count at the last bottle, minus every dose marked taken since. Skipped and refused doses don't use a pill. Never below zero. Pills per dose Read from the dose text: 2 tablets uses 2, 1/2 tablet or ½ tablet uses 0.5. Changing the dose mid-bottle starts a fresh count from what is left, on the same bottle (no second alert). Days left Today's doses that nobody has marked yet are set aside first, then whole days at the current schedule: remaining pills ÷ (times a day × pills per dose). The same bottle gives the same answer at 7 AM and at 8 PM. Paused medicines show Paused and never alert. Runs out Today + days left: the last day with every dose covered. Low Days left at or under the guardian's threshold (Remind me when a medicine has N days left, 3–14, default 7). Calendar refill When low, an orange Refill entry is added at 10:00 three days before it runs out (today if that's already past). It isn't added if a refill for that medicine is already scheduled in the window; the screens then show that entry's date. One entry per bottle. Pausing the medicine cancels the automatic entry and resuming brings it back; an entry a person cancelled stays cancelled. Alert One per bottle, to Sarah and the caregiver: "Lisinopril: 6 days left. Request a refill from Fog City Pharmacy." The lock-screen title stays "You have a reminder from Circle Care". Who can act Request refill and New bottle show only to people who may change counts, so a refused change never looks like it worked. Change requests Approving an older change request keeps today's pill count. Request refill Marks the bottle requested (who and when, on the medicine's history), stops repeats and tells the other of Sarah or the caregiver. New bottle Enter the count (quick picks 30, 60, 90; 1–1000). Resets the count, logs "New bottle: N on hand" and closes the automatic Calendar entry for the old bottle.

Where it shows: a supply row on each Medications card (bar, days left, runs out date, Request refill, New bottle), Pills on hand on the caregiver's Today (low ones first) and a Needs your attention item on the guardian dashboard. Demo seed: Atorvastatin starts at 6 days, so the alert and Calendar refill show on first load; the presenter sheet's Simulate low Metformin supply sets Metformin to 7 days.

Mockups: Sprint 12 design.

docs.title: Notes & documents
docs.text: Feature ID / area F-10 · Care notes with visibility, secure documents (/app/guardian/notes, /app/caregiver/notes) Personas Sarah (guardian), Ana (on shift), James (family) Status Built in prototype — no server-side virus scan Related stories CC-23 legal-authority upload · CC-66 care notes with visibility · CC-67 secure documents (type check, encryption, watermarked viewer) · CC-19 read guard Last updated 2026-10-19

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. A shared notebook for the circle. Anyone allowed can post a note to Everyone or to Sarah only. Documents — care plans, discharge summaries, legal papers — are checked by their real file type, encrypted on the device, and opened in a viewer that watermarks the viewer's name and the time across the page. Every view goes into Maggie's access log.

Why. Care information arrives as scattered texts and paper. Some of it is sensitive (a family concern, a legal document) and should not be visible to everyone; documents copied out of an app are a common source of leaks.

Business value. One place for the circle's context; a defensible model for sensitive documents that agencies and compliance reviewers expect.

docs.title: User journey
docs.text:
1. Sarah (or Ana while on shift) opens Notes & documents — "Shared with the circle".
  2. She writes in "Share an update with the circle…", picks Everyone or Sarah only, and taps Post note ("Note posted"). The hint explains who will see it.
  3. Notes list shows author, time ("2 days ago") and visibility (Everyone or a lock and Sarah only).
  4. Documents lists each file with type, size, uploader and date, plus Verified, In review or Resubmit badges for legal documents, and View.
  5. To upload, she picks a type (Care plan, Discharge summary, Legal authority (guardian only), Other) and taps Upload. "PDF, PNG or JPEG up to 10 MB. Files are checked, encrypted on this device and shown with the viewer's name watermarked across them. In the full product they're also virus-scanned on our servers."
  6. A wrong file type is rejected: ""fake.pdf" isn't a PDF, PNG or JPEG file. Only those types can be uploaded." A valid file is added ("Document added", or "Sent for verification" for legal authority).
  7. View opens the document with a repeating watermark such as "Sarah · Oct 19, 2026, 4:08 PM". "Watermarked for Sarah · … This view was added to Maggie's access log."
Notes with per-note visibility, and encrypted documents.

Open design question

The hint above says Maggie can see notes about her, but the permission matrix gives notes.private: read to the guardian only, and the elder app has no Notes screen. This conflicts with "her data, her decision" and possibly a right of access; it is logged as a product decision in the docs index and the permission matrix.

docs.text: Feature ID / area F-13 · Pilot recruitment, in-app feedback, pilot dashboard and demo mode Personas Prospective pilot families (website), all app personas (survey), internal product team (dashboard), presenters (demo mode) Status Built in prototype — dashboard defaults to a synthetic sample cohort Related stories CC-74 pilot with 15–25 care circles · CC-75 setup call · CC-76 in-app NPS · CC-77 pilot success dashboard · CC-80 persona switcher demo mode (approved addition) Last updated 2026-10-19

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. A Join the pilot page recruits families for an 8-week pilot. Inside the app, a one-question Net Promoter Score survey collects feedback without health details. An internal pilot dashboard shows aggregate results and hides any group smaller than five. Demo mode lets a presenter switch persona and simulate events.

Why. The product must be validated with real families before it is built for real. Research data must never mix with care data, and small pilots make individuals easy to identify.

Business value. Provides the learning loop for the roadmap: recruitment, a standard satisfaction metric and success measures (doses confirmed, check-ins, time to answer an alert) defined before the pilot starts. The full plan is in the pilot plan (CC-74).

docs.title: Join the pilot (CC-74)
docs.text:
1. /pilot — "Help us build this with your family." "We're inviting 15 to 25 care circles to use Circle Care for eight weeks next summer and tell us what works — and what doesn't."
  2. Promises: Eight weeks, starting May 2027 · A 30-minute setup call, two short check-ins, and a final conversation · Free for life for pilot families, plus a thank-you gift card · You can leave anytime. Your data is deleted when you do.
  3. Tell us about your circle: Your name, Email or phone, You are… (older adult / family member / legal guardian or POA / professional caregiver), State (e.g. California), Does a professional caregiver visit?, and consent "I agree to be contacted about the pilot. Please don't include any health information here." → Send → "Thank you, (first name). We'll reach out within two weeks to talk about whether the pilot is a good fit for your family."
Pilot recruitment page.

docs.title: In-app feedback (CC-76)
docs.text:
1. After a person's second sign-in, their home screen shows "How likely are you to recommend Circle Care to a friend or colleague?" ("to a friend" for the elder) with a 0–10 scale.

docs.text: Feature ID / area F-11 · Elder-controlled privacy (/app/elder/privacy, /app/guardian/privacy) Personas Maggie (controls), Sarah (views; can export, sign out everywhere and close the circle) Status Built in prototype Related stories CC-81 Privacy Center (approved addition) · CC-20 who can see my data · CC-21 revoke access · CC-22 consent review · CC-26 encrypted storage · CC-27 sign out everywhere · CC-28 tamper-evident log · CC-29 access history · CC-32 export my data · CC-33 close circle and delete · CC-87 health-sharing consent Last updated 2026-10-19

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. One page where the elder sees and controls her information: pause sharing, choose whether her health readings are shared, see who can see her information and who looked at it, check that the access log is intact, download an encrypted copy, review what she agreed to, sign out everywhere, and close the circle. The guardian sees the same page in read-only form for the sharing switches.

Why. "Her data. Her decision." is Circle Care's core promise. Without a place to exercise it, privacy is only a policy.

Business value. The Privacy Center is the clearest differentiator from monitoring-style competitors (competitive teardown) and directly supports HIPAA-style rights of access, accounting of disclosures and deletion.

docs.title: User journey
docs.text:
1. Maggie taps My privacy on her home screen: Your information, your choice (Sarah sees Maggie's privacy).
  2. Pause sharing — "Stops sharing with family and caregivers. SOS still works." When on: "Sharing is paused. Only SOS alerts go out." (toast "Sharing paused").
  3. Share health readings with Sarah — "Heart rate, blood oxygen, activity and sleep from your watch. Only Sarah can see them."
  4. Who can see your information lists every member with relationship, what they can see (e.g. "Today's plan, only during their shifts"), Invited and Access ends labels, and Remove (not for Sarah).
  5. Who looked at your information — the last 30 days of other people's actions: "James viewed care notes · 20 hr ago", "Ana created a shift hand-off · Yesterday".
  6. Download my data and What I agreed to ("Version 1.0, Thu, Aug 20.").
  7. Access log is intact — "All 9 entries check out. Each entry is sealed to the one before it, so any change or deletion would show up here."
  8. Open a downloaded copy and Sign out everywhere.
  9. What Circle Care keeps — counts of medicines, dose records, notes, documents and access-log entries; "Everything is encrypted, and nothing is sold or used for ads."
  10. Close this circle and delete its data.
Maggie's Privacy Center (full page, phone). Sarah's view: status badges, no switches.

docs.title: Download an encrypted copy (CC-32)
docs.text:
1. Download my data → Confirm it's you ("Downloading health information needs a quick check. The file is saved only to this device.") → Confirm with Face ID.
  2. Protect the download — "Choose a passphrase. The file is locked with it, so it's safe even if it's emailed or copied. We can't recover it for you." Passphrase (≥ 8 characters) twice → Download encrypted copy → circle-care-export-2026-10-19.ccexport ("Encrypted copy downloaded").
  3. Open a downloaded copy → choose the file, enter the passphrase → Unlock shows a summary (export time, people, medicines, dose records, notes, documents, access-log entries). A wrong passphrase: "That passphrase doesn't open "file"." Nothing is uploaded.
Exports are always passphrase-encrypted.

docs.title: Sign out everywhere (CC-27)
docs.text: 1. Sign out everywhere — "Lost a phone? This ends every session and turns off notifications on all devices." All personas are signed out, the app returns to the person picker, and Sarah is told.

docs.title: Close this circle (CC-33)
docs.text: 1. Close this circle? — "This deletes Maggie's medicines, notes, documents and schedules, removes everyone's access, and erases the encryption key on this device so no copy can be read." Type DELETE → Delete everything (or Keep the circle).

docs.title: SOS & emergency
docs.text: Feature ID / area F-03 · Emergency response Personas Maggie (raises SOS), Sarah, Ana and James (responders) Status Partially built — the full flow works in-app; real push/SMS delivery, location and 911 integration are not built Related stories CC-46 hold-to-send SOS · CC-47 call 911 · CC-48 escalation chain · CC-49 acknowledge & resolve · CC-50 critical alerts break through silent mode · CC-52 missed daily check-in · CC-53 emergency card Last updated 2026-10-19

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. Maggie presses and holds SOS. After a 10-second chance to cancel, the people on her escalation list are alerted one after another — Sarah first, then Ana after 2 minutes, then James after 4 — until someone taps "I'm on my way." Maggie sees who is coming. The responder closes the event with a note of what happened. An emergency card gives first responders her allergies, conditions, medicines and contacts, and a daily check-in catches the quieter emergencies.

Why. A single phone call to a single relative is a fragile safety net. Personal emergency buttons exist, but they rarely tell the elder who is coming, and they are disconnected from the family's daily plan.

Business value. SOS is the feature families cite first when deciding to adopt a care app. Fast, visible acknowledgement is a pilot success metric (median alert answered in under 10 minutes — see Pilot & feedback).

Not an emergency service

Every SOS screen says: "Circle Care alerts your family and caregivers. It is not a monitored emergency service — call 911 if you are in danger." A Call 911 button is always visible.

docs.title: Raising an SOS (elder)
docs.text:
1. Maggie taps the red SOS tile on her home screen.
  2. Press and hold for help — a large round button with a progress ring. "Hold for 2 seconds. Your family and Ana will be told where you are." A secondary Call 911 button sits below.
  3. When the ring completes, Sending for help in 10 counts down. If read-aloud is on she hears "Sending for help in 10 seconds. Tap cancel if you're OK."
  4. She can tap Cancel — I'm OK ("Cancelled. No one was alerted.") or Send now.
  5. At zero, Help is on the way — "We're telling your family now." Who we're telling lists each person: Alerted, In 2 min if no answer, In 4 min if no answer.
Hold-to-send prevents accidental alerts. 10 seconds to cancel. The escalation chain, as Maggie sees it.

docs.title: Responding (guardian, caregiver, family)
docs.text:
1. Every guardian and caregiver screen shows a red bar: Maggie pressed SOS at 4:08 PM · Respond. A critical banner also appears.
  2. The responder screen: Maggie needs help — "Pressed SOS at 4:08 PM · Just now", location "At home · 412 Elizabeth St, Noe Valley, San Francisco (demo address)", buttons I'm on my way, Call Maggie and Call 911, and the escalation list with Alerted / Next / Responding badges.
  3. Tapping I'm on my way stops escalation and notifies everyone: "Sarah is responding to Maggie's SOS."
  4. Maggie's screen switches to the responder's photo and "Sarah is coming" — "Stay where you are if you can. Sarah answered at 4:09 PM."
  5. The SOS is closed either by Maggie (I'm OK now, recorded as "Resolved by Maggie — Sarah arrived.") or by the responder, who must type What happened? (required to close) and tap Mark resolved.
  6. With no active SOS, the responder page shows No active SOS — "Maggie is OK. If she presses SOS, you'll get an alert that breaks through silent mode." — and a list of Past alerts with outcomes.
The responder view on a phone.

docs.title: Emergency card (CC-53)
docs.text:
1. Emergency card (elder home link, caregiver tab, guardian menu) shows a red-topped card: name, age, blood type, Allergies (in red), Conditions, Current medicines (all non-paused medicines with strength), Decisions (directives) and one-tap calls to the first two people on the SOS list.
  2. The footer states "Approved by Maggie on …" or "Waiting for Maggie to approve".
  3. Edit: Maggie's edits save immediately. Sarah's edits are sent as Send to Maggie — "Maggie must approve changes before they appear on her card."
  4. Lock-screen code shows an example QR code: "Responders scan this code from Maggie's lock screen to open the card for 1 hour. Each scan is added to the access log."
The emergency card is approved by Maggie and every view is logged.

docs.title: Missed daily check-in (CC-52)
docs.text:
1. If Maggie has not tapped I'm OK by the end of her check-in window (default 10:00 AM), she gets one more gentle prompt.
  2. Fifteen minutes later, Sarah is alerted and her home screen shows Maggie hasn't checked in — "Window ended at 10:00 AM — consider calling."

docs.title: Website & onboarding
docs.text: Feature ID / area F-01 · Acquisition, identity and first run Personas Prospective families and caregivers (website); Maggie, Ana, Sarah (sign-in); invited members such as Ruth Status Built in prototype — identity is simulated (no real accounts, SMS or biometrics) Related stories CC-11 sign up & sign in · CC-12 MFA · CC-13 elder-friendly sign-in · CC-14 session lock · CC-15 create a circle · CC-17 accept an invitation · CC-22 consent · CC-75 welcome tour & setup call Last updated 2026-10-19

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. A six-page marketing website that explains the product, followed by the app's entry flow: choose a person, sign in (with a second step for caregivers and guardians), accept the privacy agreement (elder), take a short welcome tour, and — for invited helpers — accept an invitation.

Why. Families decide whether to trust a care app before they install it. The website states the privacy promise in plain language up front. Inside the app, sign-in must be strong enough for health information yet simple enough for an 80-year-old.

Business value. Converts visitors into pilot sign-ups (Pilot & feedback), sets expectations about privacy before any data is entered, and reduces setup support through the welcome tour and a free setup call.

docs.title: Marketing website
docs.text:
1. A visitor lands on Home (/): "Care, in one circle." with Try the demo and See how it works.
  2. How it works (/how-it-works) tells one ordinary day in Maggie's circle as a timeline (Ana checks in 8:02 AM → doses verified 8:06 → Maggie's "I'm OK" 8:40 → spoken reminder 12:30 PM → SOS 1:35 PM → "I'm on my way" 1:36 → self-writing hand-off 2:00 PM → Sunday digest), then three setup steps: Create the circle, Invite helpers by role, Verify the guardian.
  3. Features (/features) shows the feature list per person behind tabs For Maggie / For Ana / For Sarah.
  4. Who it's for (/who-its-for) gives each persona's promise and a hypothesis quote marked "Design hypothesis · to be validated in interviews".
  5. Privacy (/privacy) lists eight privacy pillars, six "Things we will never do", and five FAQs.
  6. Join the pilot (/pilot) collects interest (see Pilot & feedback).
  7. A translucent top navigation and footer appear on every page; on phones the links collapse into a menu button.
How it works — one day in Maggie's circle. Features — the same plan shown three ways. Who it's for. Privacy — pillars, "never" list and FAQs.

docs.title: Entering the app
docs.text:
1. Try the demo or Open the app goes to /app, Welcome to Circle Care: "This demo has one care circle with three people in it. Pick who you'd like to be — you can switch anytime."
  2. The visitor picks Maggie (Elder), Ana (Caregiver) or Sarah (Legal guardian). If that person is already signed in, the app opens directly.
Choose a person. "Start a new care circle" opens the sign-up flow.

docs.title: Sign-in and MFA (caregiver and guardian)
docs.text:
1. Hi, Sarah — "Sign in to Maggie's care circle." Email and password are prefilled for the demo. Continue.
  2. "New device detected — we'll ask for a second step to keep Maggie's information safe." The next screen asks: "Enter the code we sent to your phone." — "Sent to •••• 0177. Demo code: 482913".
  3. A correct code signs the person in and opens their home screen.
Step 1: email and password. Step 2: six-digit code.

docs.title: Elder sign-in and consent
docs.text:
1. Maggie's screen says "Sign in with your face — no password needed." Tapping Sign in with Face ID shows Looking… then Welcome back (an animation in the demo).
  2. Hint: "Lost your phone? Sarah can help you sign in on a new one — she'll need to confirm it's you."
  3. If Maggie has never agreed to the privacy terms, Here is how Circle Care works appears with four plain-language points, a Read this to me button and I understand and agree. (The seeded demo already has consent, so this step is skipped unless consent is cleared.)

docs.title: Welcome tour and setup call
docs.text:
1. The first time each persona opens the app, a Getting started sheet shows 3–4 short cards with Next / Skip.
  2. The last card offers Start using Circle Care and I'd like a free setup call → toast "We'll call within one business day to help set up".
The welcome tour (CC-75).

docs.title: Start a new care circle (sign-up)
docs.text: 1. Start a new care circle on the Welcome screen opens a three-step sheet: Create your account (name, email or mobile, password with a strength meter, privacy-notice checkbox) → Verify it's you (6-digit code) → Create a care circle (Who is this circle for?, Your role). The demo then opens Sarah's example circle.

docs.title: Invitation acceptance
docs.text:
1. An invited person opens /#/app/invite/<memberId>: "Sarah invited you to Maggie's care circle", their role and end date, and What you'll be able to see for their role.
  2. Accept invitation → "Welcome to the circle". If more than 72 hours have passed: "This invitation expired after 72 hours" and Ask Sarah for a new link.

The four consent points, verbatim:

  1. You choose who is in your circle. You can remove people anytime.
  2. Each person only sees what they need to help you. You can see who looked at your information.
  3. You can pause sharing with one switch. Emergency alerts still work.
  4. If you press SOS, we tell your family and caregivers right away.

docs.text:
• Each persona signs in separately; the welcome screen shows "Fictional demo data, stored only in this browser."

The website collects nothing except the optional pilot form. The pilot form keeps only role, state and whether a paid caregiver visits; name and contact are discarded in the prototype (see Pilot & feedback).

docs.title: Demo guide
docs.text:
A step-by-step script for a five-minute live demo of the Circle Care prototype, followed by a reference of every presenter control. Use it for stakeholder reviews, sprint reviews, portfolio walk-throughs and interviews.

Before you start

  • Open the demo in a desktop browser (wide layout) or on a phone (tab-bar layout). Both work.
  • Open Demo · Name → Reset demo so the data matches this script.
  • Demo MFA code: 482913 (tap the code on the screen to fill it).
  • The demo clock is real local time plus any time you skip ahead. What is "due" depends on when you present; the script works best between about 9:00 AM and 2:00 PM, when Ana is on shift.

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text: You want Go to Website /#/ (plus /#/how-it-works, /#/features, /#/who-its-for, /#/privacy, /#/pilot) Choose a person /#/app Switch person or use presenter controls The Demo · Name pill, top right of the app Review team console /#/app/review (or Demo mode → Review team console) Pilot dashboard /#/app/pilot (or Demo mode → Pilot dashboard)

docs.title: 0:00 — Set the scene (website)
docs.text:
1. Open the website home page. Read the headline: "Care, in one circle." One sentence: an older adult, their caregivers and their legal guardian on the same page — with the elder in charge of who sees what.
  2. Click Try the demo.

docs.title: 0:30 — Choose a person and sign in
docs.text:
1. On Welcome to Circle Care, point out the three people: Maggie (Elder), Ana (Caregiver), Sarah (Legal guardian). Click Sarah.
  2. Sign-in is prefilled. Click Continue, then enter 482913 (or tap the demo code) and Sign in. Mention: "New device detected — we'll ask for a second step."
  3. If the Getting started tour appears, click Skip (or show one card).
Guardian and caregiver sign-in. Second step: 6-digit code.

docs.title: 1:00 — Guardian: today at a glance
docs.text:
1. On Sarah's Home, read the headline (e.g. "3 things need you.") and the North Star line.
  2. Walk the tiles: Check-in, Medicines ring, Tasks, With Maggie now, Health, Next appointment, Alerts — "Notifications never show health details."
  3. Point at Needs your attention: unread hand-off, pending approvals, uncovered shifts.
Sarah's dashboard: everything that matters today on one screen.

docs.title: 1:45 — Elder: SOS
docs.text:
1. Open Demo · Sarah → Margaret Lee to switch to Maggie. Show the three big buttons.
  2. Tap SOS, then press and hold the round SOS button for 2 seconds. The "Sending for help in 10" countdown starts; mention Cancel — I'm OK. Tap Send now (or wait).
  3. Maggie sees "Help is on the way" and Who we're telling: Sarah Alerted, Ana In 2 min if no answer, James In 4 min if no answer.
10 seconds to cancel. Escalation chain shown to Maggie.

docs.title: 2:30 — Guardian responds
docs.text:
1. Switch to Sarah. A red bar reads "Maggie pressed SOS". Tap Respond and then I'm on my way.
  2. Switch back to Maggie: her screen now says "Sarah is coming". Tap I'm OK now to close the SOS (or close it as Sarah with an outcome note).
The responder view (phone layout).

docs.title: 3:15 — A missed dose escalates
docs.text:
1. Open Demo mode → Simulate a missed dose. Lisinopril (high priority) is now 70 minutes late, past both escalation thresholds.
  2. As Sarah, Home shows "Lisinopril not confirmed · … · high priority" and a new alert.

docs.title: 3:45 — Caregiver: give the dose and hand off
docs.text:
1. Switch to Ana. (If she is not on shift, tap Check in → Check in — I'm here.)
  2. On Today, find Lisinopril marked Overdue; tap Given. Point out "Given by Ana at … ✓" — a caregiver-verified dose.
  3. Optionally tap I've read this on James's hand-off.
  4. Tap End shift. The Hand-off screen shows a summary "Drafted from your shift". Pick a mood and tap Send hand-off and check out.
The self-drafting hand-off. Nothing is sent until Ana confirms.

docs.title: 4:30 — Close on privacy
docs.text:
1. Switch to Maggie → My privacy. Show Pause sharing, Share health readings with Sarah, Who can see your information and Who looked at your information.
  2. Close with the three principles: privacy-first, elder in control, minimum necessary.

Shorter version (3 minutes)

Steps 9–13 (SOS round trip), 14–15 (missed dose) and 16–19 (hand-off). This is the script in the repository README.

docs.title: About the product
docs.text:
What is Circle Care, in one sentence?

A care-coordination app that keeps an older adult, their caregivers and their legal guardian on the same daily plan, with the older adult in charge of who sees what.

Is Circle Care a real, available product?

No. It is a concept product built by Sumanth as a Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO) training assignment and portfolio piece. The working prototype demonstrates the experience; it is not offered to the public and must not be used with real health information.

Who is it for?

Older adults who live at home and want help without losing independence; the professional and family caregivers who support them; and the legal guardian or healthcare power of attorney who makes decisions with them. See Personas.

How is it different from a medication reminder app or a family group chat?

It combines the pieces that usually live in separate tools — medicine schedules, caregiver shifts, check-ins, emergencies and decisions — around one person, and gives that person real control: a Privacy Center, an access log, one-tap pause, and visibility of every decision. Caregivers see care details only during their shifts. The competitive teardown frames the positioning to be validated.

What is the North Star metric?

Verified care tasks completed on time per week. In the prototype that is doses recorded as taken within 60 minutes of their scheduled time, plus completed care tasks, over the last 7 days. It is shown on the guardian's home screen and weekly digest.

docs.title: About the prototype
docs.text:
Is any of the data real?

No. Maggie, Sarah, Ana, James and Ruth are fictional. Phone numbers use the reserved 555-01xx range. Health readings are generated by a formula. Nothing leaves your browser.

Where is the data stored?

In your browser's local storage, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key that the browser will not let any script read or export. Each browser has its own separate copy. See Security & privacy.

What is the MFA code?

482913 — for every sign-in and for the sign-up flow. You can also tap the code on screen to fill it in.

Do notifications actually get sent?

No. The prototype shows in-app banners and an Alerts list. Real push, SMS and email delivery is planned for production.

Does the app use my location, camera or microphone?

Location: no — check-in shows the flow but does not read GPS. Microphone: only if you tap Answer with my voice on a reminder and your browser can recognise speech on the device; if recognition would need a cloud service, the feature stays off. Camera: no.

Why are some photos blank?

Stock photos are loaded from Unsplash and need internet access. Without it, they show as soft placeholders or coloured circles.

Can I install it on my phone?

Yes. Open the deployed URL in Safari (iOS) or Chrome (Android) and choose Share → Add to Home Screen. It opens full-screen and works offline after the first visit.

How do I reset everything?

Demo · Name → Reset demo. To also destroy the encryption key and uploaded files, use Privacy Center → Close this circle and delete its data as Maggie or Sarah.

docs.title: Privacy and compliance
docs.text:
Is Circle Care HIPAA compliant?

The prototype is designed to the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules, but it is not a production system and has not been assessed. Whether HIPAA legally applies depends on the business model: a consumer app families use directly is usually covered by the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule and state privacy laws instead; selling to home care agencies would make Circle Care a business associate. See the regulatory memo and HIPAA risk analysis.

Who can see Maggie's medicines?

Maggie, Sarah (her verified guardian), family members in her circle, and professional caregivers only while checked in to a shift. When Maggie pauses sharing, family and caregivers lose access to everything except SOS, the emergency card and the circle list. See the permission matrix.

Why does the guardian keep access when Maggie pauses sharing?

A healthcare power of attorney carries legal authority. The guardian keeps access but is told sharing is paused. Health readings are the exception: Maggie can stop sharing those with Sarah separately.

Can Maggie remove her guardian from the circle?

Not in the app. The Privacy Center explains that Sarah's access can only be changed through the legal process. Maggie can remove anyone else.

Is Circle Care a medical device or an emergency service?

No. The Health page and SOS screens say so explicitly: "Circle Care isn't a medical device; call 911 in an emergency" and "It is not a monitored emergency service — call 911 if you are in danger."

docs.title: About this wiki
docs.text:
What happens when the wiki and the code disagree?

The code wins. Raise a change to the wiki (see How to contribute).

Where are the user stories?

In the Notion Circle Care — Product Hub. Story IDs (CC-n) appear in code comments and throughout this wiki; the traceability matrix maps them to pages, files and tests.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms used across the product, the code and this wiki. Code identifiers are shown in monospace where a term maps directly to the data model.

Term Meaning Access log The record of who viewed, created, changed, approved, exported or was refused what, and when (AuditEvent). Shown to the elder and guardian in the Privacy Center. It holds no readings or note text, but it can name a medicine, a document or an appointment, so it is protected as PHI. See Tamper-evident. Acknowledge (hand-off) The next caregiver tapping I've read this on the previous shift's hand-off. Unread hand-offs appear on the guardian's attention list. Acknowledge (SOS) A responder tapping I'm on my way. This stops escalation and tells the elder who is coming. Adherence Share of scheduled doses recorded as taken. Shown per day in the weekly digest. Alert An in-app notification (Alert) with a PHI-free title (what the lock screen would show) and an in-app detail. Has a severity: info, warning or critical. Approval A request that waits for the guardian's decision: a medicine change, a new member or a shift swap (Approval.kind). The elder sees every decision. BAA Business Associate Agreement — the HIPAA contract required with any vendor that handles protected health information for a covered entity. Tracked in the vendor register. Care circle The elder plus everyone helping them: guardian, family and professional caregivers. One circle per elder. Care task / routine A recurring non-medicine activity such as breakfast, a shower or a walk (CareTask), daily, weekdays or weekends, assigned to the caregiver on shift or to the elder. Check-in (daily) The elder's one-tap I'm OK each morning, optionally with a mood. Expected inside the check-in window (default 08:00–10:00). Check-in / check-out (visit) A professional caregiver confirming arrival and departure for a shift (Visit.checkIn / checkOut). Location is confirmed once at each, or a manual reason is recorded. Consent The elder's agreement to the plain-language privacy terms (version and time stored). A verified guardian can accept on her behalf with a written reason. Coverage gap A scheduled shift with no caregiver assigned or not yet accepted. Critical alert An alert that breaks through silent mode (SOS, missed high-priority doses) when Emergencies break through silent mode is on. In the prototype this is a setting only; delivery is not built. Demo mode The Demo · Name pill at the top of the app, which opens the persona switcher and presenter controls (CC-80). Escalation (dose) An unconfirmed dose alerts the caregiver after 30 minutes and the guardian after 60 minutes by default; high-priority medicines escalate twice as fast (15 and 30 minutes). Escalation chain (SOS) The ordered list of people alerted when the elder presses SOS (default Sarah → Ana → James). The next person is added every 2 minutes until someone acknowledges. Elder The older adult the circle is built around. In the demo, Maggie. Emergency card A first-responder summary (allergies, conditions, medicines, directives, contacts) that the elder approves. Guardian / legal guardian The person with legal authority to make health decisions with or for the elder — here, Sarah as healthcare POA. Gets guardian permissions only after the review team verifies their documents. Hand-off The end-of-shift summary a caregiver sends at check-out: mood, meals, concerns, notes and a summary (Handoff). The prototype drafts the summary automatically (CC-82). High-priority medicine A medicine flagged critical (Lisinopril in the demo). Missed doses escalate twice as fast and are marked critical. HIPAA The US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. Circle Care is designed to its Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules; whether it legally applies depends on the business model (see the regulatory memo). k-anonymity (minimum cohort) On the pilot dashboard, any group with fewer than 5 responses is hidden so no one can be singled out. Minimum necessary The HIPAA principle that each person sees only the information needed for their role. In Circle Care, caregivers see care details only during shifts. MFA Multi-factor authentication — the 6-digit code step after the password. Demo code 482913. North Star The single metric the product optimises: verified care tasks completed on time this week (doses taken within 60 minutes of schedule plus completed care tasks over the last 7 days). NPS Net Promoter Score: % of 9–10 scores minus % of 0–6 scores, from −100 to 100. Collected in-app (CC-76). On shift (pro@shift) A professional caregiver with a check-in today and no check-out. The permission matrix grants care-detail access only in this state. Pause sharing The elder's one switch that limits family and caregivers to SOS, the emergency card and the circle list (CC-81). The guardian keeps access. PHI Protected health information — health data that identifies a person. Circle Care keeps PHI out of notifications, emails, the audit log and pilot data. POA (healthcare power of attorney) A legal document naming someone to make health decisions for a person. Sarah's POA is the demo's legal-authority document. Presenter controls Buttons in demo mode that fast-forward time or simulate events (missed dose, late caregiver, SOS…). Privacy Center The elder's (and guardian's) page for who can see her information, the access log, sharing switches, export, sign-out everywhere and closing the circle. Privacy shield A blank cover that replaces the screen when the app goes to the background so the app-switcher snapshot shows no health data. PWA Progressive Web App — a website that can be installed to a phone's home screen and opened offline after the first visit. Respite caregiver A temporary caregiver who covers for the usual one. Ruth in the demo, with 14-day access. Review team Internal Trust & Safety staff who verify legal-authority documents (CC-24). Rules engine The evaluate() function in src/data/store.tsx that turns time and state into alerts (missed doses, check-ins, late caregivers, SOS steps, reminders, suspicious access, abnormal vitals, access expiry). Runs every 15 seconds and after every change. Session lock The app locks after inactivity: 15 minutes by default for caregiver and guardian; off by default for the elder, who can choose 5 or 15 minutes. Suspicious access 8 or more record views by one person within 5 minutes, or 3 or more refused actions within 10 minutes, which alert the guardian (CC-35). Tamper-evident Each access-log entry stores a SHA-256 hash of itself and of the previous entry, so editing, deleting or reordering any entry breaks the chain and is detected. Time-limited access A member's expiresOn date after which their access is revoked automatically (CC-25). Verified dose A dose recorded by a caregiver who was checked in at the time (DoseLog.verified). Vitals Heart rate and blood oxygen readings from the elder's watch — simulated in the prototype every 30 minutes. Weekly digest The guardian's weekly summary: adherence, visits, check-in streak, North Star, and anything worth knowing. The email version contains no PHI (CC-83).

docs.title: Personas
docs.text:
Circle Care is designed around one care circle: an older adult at the centre and the people who help them. The prototype ships with one fictional circle in San Francisco, California. Each persona below is a design persona — the goals and pains are hypotheses to be validated by the research plan (CC-1 to CC-5), not findings from real interviews.

All personas are fictional

Names, relationships, phone numbers (+1 (415) 555-01xx) and health details are invented for the demo. Any resemblance to real people is coincidental.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Persona Demo person Role in code (Member.role) Signs in with Colour Elder Margaret "Maggie" Lee, 80 elder Face ID-style sign-in (no password) Sunrise orange Legal guardian Sarah Lee, daughter, healthcare power of attorney guardian (verified) Email + password + 6-digit code Indigo Professional caregiver Ana Rivera, home care aide pro Email + password + 6-digit code Teal Family member James Lee, grandson family (No dedicated app view in the demo) Green Respite caregiver Ruth Okafor pro, time-limited, invite pending Invitation link Pink Review team Internal Trust & Safety reviewer (actor trust-safety) Internal console —

The demo has three app experiences — elder, caregiver and guardian. James and Ruth appear in the circle, the SOS chain, shift swaps and approvals, but you cannot sign in as them.

The demo's "Welcome to Circle Care" screen: pick who you want to be. You can switch at any time.

docs.title: Maggie Lee — the elder
docs.text:
Margaret "Maggie" Lee, 80. Widowed, lives alone in her own home in San Francisco. Takes four medicines (blood pressure, blood sugar, vitamin D, cholesterol). Wears a watch that could share heart rate and activity. Still makes her own decisions.

Goals Stay in her own home. Remember her medicines without feeling nagged. Be able to get help fast. Keep her dignity and privacy. Pains Small text and busy screens. Feeling watched. Daily "just checking" phone calls. Not knowing what her family decided about her care. Quote (hypothesis) "I don't want to be watched. I want to be able to ask for help." What she uses Elder home (What's next, SOS, Call my person), reminders with read-aloud and voice answers, daily "I'm OK", Updates about me, Privacy Center, Emergency card, text size and lock settings. Permissions summary Reads everything about herself except guardian-only notes and caregiver hand-offs. Records her own doses and tasks (the matrix also lets her edit medicines, though the elder app offers no screen for it). Owns her emergency card. Invites and removes members (not her guardian). Pauses sharing, controls health-reading sharing, exports and deletes data. Cannot change guardian settings such as alert timing.

docs.title: Sarah Lee — the legal guardian
docs.text:
Sarah Lee, Maggie's daughter, holds a healthcare power of attorney (verified by the review team). Lives about two hours away, works full-time.

Goals Know Maggie is OK without calling three times a day. Make the important decisions (medicine changes, who joins the circle). Fill gaps in the caregiver schedule before they happen. Pains Finds out about problems days later, from someone else. Too many messages, none of them structured. Responsible for decisions without the information to make them. Quote (hypothesis) "I find out about problems days later, from someone else." What she uses Guardian dashboard, approvals, activity, digest and settings, Health, Calendar, Medications, Shift schedule, Care circle, Notes & documents, Alerts, SOS responder. Permissions summary Reads everything, including guardian-only notes. Writes medicines, schedule, appointments and settings directly. Approves or declines requests. Invites and revokes members. Can edit the emergency card, but her changes wait for Maggie's approval before they count as approved. Sees health readings only while Maggie shares them. Keeps access when Maggie pauses sharing. Can accept the privacy agreement on Maggie's behalf only once verified and with a written reason.

docs.title: Ana Rivera — the professional caregiver
docs.text:
Ana Rivera, home care aide from an agency. Works Monday to Saturday, 8:00 AM–2:00 PM. Uses her own phone, sometimes a shared one.

Goals Walk in and know exactly what this shift needs. Prove what she did. Hand off cleanly without writing an essay. Pains "Half my morning is figuring out what happened yesterday." Paper logs. Being blamed for missed doses she never knew about. What she uses Caregiver Today (check-in, doses, tasks), the end-of-shift hand-off, Schedule, Notes (on shift only), Emergency card, Alerts, SOS responder. Permissions summary Minimum necessary. Off shift she sees only the circle, the schedule, hand-offs, the emergency card, appointments and SOS. While checked in she can read medicines, doses, tasks, notes and documents, record doses and tasks, write hand-offs and guardian-only notes, and propose medicine changes. She can never approve, export, delete or see the digest or access log.

docs.title: James Lee — family member
docs.text:
James Lee, Maggie's grandson. Covers Sunday 10:00 AM–4:00 PM and is third in the SOS chain.

Goals Help on weekends without being the one in charge. Know what happened during the week. Pains Doesn't know what changed since last Sunday. What he uses (in the circle) Appears in hand-offs, SOS escalation, shift-swap targets and approvals (he requested Ruth's respite access). No dedicated sign-in view in the demo. Permissions summary Reads today's medicines, doses, tasks, notes, documents, history and appointments. Records doses and tasks, proposes medicine and schedule changes, responds to SOS. Loses everything except SOS, emergency card and circle when Maggie pauses sharing.

docs.title: Ruth Okafor — respite caregiver (time-limited)
docs.text: Ruth is invited to cover Ana's vacation. Her access is pending (she hasn't accepted yet and Sarah hasn't approved the request) and is set to end automatically after 14 days. She illustrates time-bound access (CC-25) and the invitation flow (CC-17).

docs.title: Review team — internal

docs.title: v0.6 — Everyday Care (Sprint 12)
docs.text: Stories: CC-120, CC-121, CC-142, CC-143, CC-164, CC-165, CC-191 · Team: Dev Agent (developer), QA Agent (tester), Release Agent (build & deploy), Lead Architect Agent (approver), Sumanth (PO) · Design: mockups

docs.title: Feature 1 — Refill tracker and low-supply alerts (CC-120, CC-121)
docs.text:
• Pills on hand for each medicine, counted when a bottle is opened and reduced by each dose marked taken.
  • Days left and the day it runs out, on Medications and the caregiver's Today.
  • Low-supply alert at a threshold Sarah picks (3 to 14 days), once per bottle, with a Refill entry added to the Calendar 3 days before it runs out.
  • Request refill and New bottle actions, logged on the medicine's history and in the access log.
  • New supply resource in the permission matrix: paid caregivers see and update counts only on shift.
  • Review: approved after three rounds of changes.
  • Saved demo data moves to version 7 (older saved data is replaced with the new demo seed).

docs.title: Feature 2 — One-tap daily check-ins (CC-142, CC-143)
docs.text:
• My day card on Maggie's home: how she feels (six drawn faces, no emoji), glasses of water and meals. Every tap saves, and all of it is optional.
  • One gentle reminder at 7 PM, only on a day she added nothing.
  • Daily check-ins · 7 days in Sarah's Health summary, and today's line on her Check-in tile, only while Maggie shares them.
  • No meals for 2 days sends Sarah one gentle note.
  • Share daily check-ins with Sarah switch in Maggie's Privacy Center. Only she can change it; Sarah is told either way.
  • New wellbeing resource in the permission matrix: Maggie writes, Sarah reads only while shared, nobody else sees it.
  • The "I'm OK" check-in no longer stores an emoji mood.
  • Review: docs/reviews/2026-11-14-sprint-12-daily-checkins.md.
  • Saved demo data moves to version 8.

docs.title: Feature 3 — Private family chat (CC-164, CC-165)
docs.text:
• Family chat for Maggie, Sarah and James: one shared conversation, newest at the bottom, with an unread count on Sarah's new Chat tab. The header says exactly who can read it.
  • Lock screen only says "New message in Circle Care". The words show inside the app.
  • Health-detail check: a message that names one of Maggie's medicines, a diagnosis or a dose (like 10 mg) offers Save as a note, Send anyway or Edit first. Only the sender sees the check.
  • Messages are 1 to 1000 characters; longer ones are refused with a count, never cut.
  • Maggie's view: 22 point bubbles, one big microphone, and a You said card with Send and Try again, so nothing goes until she taps Send. She can type instead, and the typing box opens by itself where the device has no speech recognition. Her messages show By voice.
  • Chat tile on Maggie's home with the newest message and an Open chat button. Show chat on my home in her settings hides it; only she can change it, and the chat stays under Family.
  • Paid caregivers join only when Maggie or Sarah switches them on under People, and then get a Chat tab. Switching off, leaving the circle or a time limit ending removes access at once. Attempts from outside the chat are refused and logged.
  • New chat resource in the permission matrix. A caregiver who is added sees messages from the time they joined, not the history before.
  • Review: docs/reviews/2026-11-14-sprint-12-family-chat.md.
  • Design: Figma board, approved by Sumanth on 2026-11-14.
  • Saved demo data moves to version 10.

docs.title: Feature 4 — Evening recap for Sarah (CC-191)
docs.text:
• Evening recap card on Sarah's Home from 6 PM: one headline ("A calm day for Maggie." only when every dose so far is confirmed, the check-in is done and no refill is open; otherwise what needs a look), then Medicines, Check-in, Visits, Her day and Tomorrow.
  • Medicines gives doses given so far, then names each dose not confirmed, skipped or refused with its time, and any dose due now. On a calm day it gives the next dose.
  • Her day shows Maggie's feeling, water and meals only while she shares them, and reads Private on a day she keeps to herself.
  • Tomorrow shows the first appointment and its prep note, or the first caregiver visit, or Nothing booked.
  • A low supply line links to Medicines and gives the refill date when it is on the Calendar, or says it isn't on the Calendar yet. See the week opens the weekly digest, and Review medicines shows on a day with a dose that needs a look, a dose due now or a refill to sort out.
  • One update at 7 PM: the lock screen says only "Update from Circle Care" and the app says "Your evening recap is ready." Sarah can turn it off under Settings · Evening recap, and it is skipped for the evening when her quiet hours cover 7 PM. If the app first runs later that evening, the update still goes out until 11 PM, outside quiet hours. The card shows either way.
  • Presenter control Skip to 7 PM for the evening recap.
  • Review: docs/reviews/2026-11-14-sprint-12-evening-recap.md.
  • Design: Figma board, approved by Sumanth on 2026-11-14.
  • Saved demo data moves to version 11.

docs.title: v0.5 — Accounts, identity & payments (Sprint 11)
docs.text: Stories: CC-172 – CC-190 · Team: Dev Agent (developer), QA Agent (tester), Release Agent (build & deploy), Lead Architect Agent (approver), Sumanth (PO) · Review: approved after one round

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Server and database. Express API with PostgreSQL (Replit PostgreSQL via DATABASE_URL; embedded Postgres for local development and tests) and versioned migrations.
  • Real accounts. Role picker (elder, caregiver, legal guardian), sign-up, sign-in, 30-minute idle / 12-hour sessions, and a 5-attempt lockout.
  • Separate persona records. Elders, caregivers and guardians each have their own table: first and last name, contact number, email.
  • Profile photo. Cropped and stripped of location data on the device, stored encrypted.
  • Social Security number for every role. AES-256-GCM encryption, last four digits only, duplicate detection, password needed to change it.
  • Guardian payments. A mandatory bank account for no-fee ACH, plus up to 5 credit or debit cards with one primary, through a Stripe-ready simulated vault (tokens and last four only).
  • Lower-environment guard. Development, test and staging accept only test SSNs, bank numbers and cards. Production refuses to start without keys, Postgres and Stripe.
  • Audit. Append-only audit log, Security · recent activity in My account, and npm run audit:export for masked FDIC and legal audit packages.
  • Wiki page Accounts, identity & payments, plus server sections in Data model and Security & privacy.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The site header shows Sign in and Get started, or My account when signed in. The demo is still available.
  • The service worker never caches /api or /vault responses.
  • Replit now deploys as an Autoscale server (APP_ENV=staging) instead of a static site.
  • Caregiver header text contrast was fixed (it was flagged by axe at certain times of day).
  • The demo end-to-end suite pins the clock to a weekday afternoon so its results don't depend on when it runs.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
• Payments don't move money yet; production needs the Stripe adapter.
  • There is no MFA, password reset or email verification for real accounts yet, and accounts aren't linked into a shared care circle.

docs.title: v0.3 — Health & Calendar
docs.text: Commits: 1dc1731 Run the dev server on port 5000 to match Replit's preview, dce35c2 Add guardian Health and Calendar features, 6c139a3 Point weight helpers at story CC-93

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Health (CC-84 – CC-93) for the guardian: a summary of highlights; heart-rate and blood-oxygen charts with a new simulated reading every 30 minutes (15/30/60 configurable); detection of high, low and sudden-change readings with guardian alerts; an accessible readings table; 30-day weight; activity rings, an hour-by-hour day strip, steps by hour, sleep stages and 7-day mood. See Health insights.
  • Health sharing consent (CC-87): Maggie controls whether Sarah sees health readings, from her Privacy Center. Only Maggie and Sarah can ever see readings.
  • Calendar (CC-94 – CC-98): a full-month view of medication-related appointments with colour and icon per type, a month legend, an "Up next" banner, multiple appointments per day, day details (provider, medicines, escort, preparation), and add / edit / mark done / cancel. See Care calendar.
  • Guardian Home tiles for Health and Next appointment; guardian Settings section for Health readings thresholds.
  • Presenter controls: Simulate a sudden heart-rate change and Simulate a low blood-oxygen reading.
